utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, as we start here, for the record, your full and complete name is -- and forgive me if I don't pronounce all these correctly -- David Nigel Pinder-Koehnk?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last part of the hyphenated last name being "K-o-e-h-n-k"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. It's actually "K-o umlaut," but it's normally written "o-e," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear and so people know exactly how to refer to you, but you typically simply go by the last name "Pinder"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. Most Britons can't actually pronounce the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, is it correct that you were a career officer in the British armed forces from May of 1965 until February of 1994, when at that time you retired from the British army with the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during this time of service you received five medals in connection or in relation to various campaigns or combat operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you are currently the director of the Council for Education in World Citizenship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long have you been in that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Since March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the events that bring us to court today, is it correct, sir, that you arrived in Central Bosnia as part of the UNPROFOR headquarters unit in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to jump to the other end of your tenure, you left Bosnia then in approximately early March of 1993 and returned to NATO duties in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As I understand it, sir, is it correct that you were the head of public affairs for UNPROFOR, based at the headquarters of the Bosnia and Herzegovina command, which at that time, and I think thereafter, was based in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. Initially we went to Zagreb, then Belgrade, and from Belgrade to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Only a matter of a week, and about a week in Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you were based, for the remainder of your duty, in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the chief of staff at UNPROFOR headquarters at that time was British Brigadier Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that your main task was to establish a press centre and a system for informing the international press, which also involved you in contacts with the local media and public officials in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the main part of the task. But equally, as the press spokesman and advisor, I was required, when possible, to inform the commanders of what was happening and being said in the local media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in that respect, is it fair to say that it was -- part of what you tried to do was keep yourself pretty well informed as to what was happening on the ground, both in terms of events on the ground and in terms of local media and local information?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your primary -- well, excuse me; your area of responsibility covered UNPROFOR's entire mission area, but is it correct that your main involvement was in Central Bosnia and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Technically that's correct. I was responsible for the whole UNPROFOR area, but because of the terrain, various operational situations, in practice, most of my time was spent with Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us, Mr. Pinder, you had approximately almost 30 years service in the British army; is that correct? The British armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Probably nearer 25 than 30, but yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with carrying out the task, some might say, well, it was a public-information role as opposed to a combat role, but did your task, your assignments, require you to be knowledgeable and keep yourself informed of the day-to-day events on the ground in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It was considered essential that I did, and to that extent I was a member of the inner command group of -- now General Cordy-Simpson, but then Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "inner command group," can you just, for us not in the military, give further explanation as to what that meant?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It was a small group of officers who daily met with Cordy-Simpson, discussed and gave opinions on the activities on the ground and the operations of UNPROFOR. So it was in fact a very small group around the brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pinder, is it correct that the first time you heard the name or heard of Dario Kordic, it was in a political context, and you came to understand that he had a high position in the hierarchy of something called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it also correct, then, in about October early November of 1992, you were invited, in your role as chief of public information or public affairs, to attend press or information conferences which were organised and presented by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. I had begun to develop contacts essentially around the Kiseljak area. As a result of that, Colonel Blaskic invited me to attend conferences held by themselves, and it was at one of those that I was introduced to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall briefly how you first came to meet Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The headquarters in Kiseljak appeared to fall under the operational area of Colonel Blaskic, so from the very first, as we moved in and negotiated that move in, Colonel Blaskic had been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I think you just mentioned a moment ago that -- it's correct, is it not, sir, that it was Colonel Blaskic who invited you to the first of these press conferences?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, was it also Colonel Blaskic who introduced you for the first time to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you in fact, subsequent to this first press conference, attend a number of similar press conferences over the next few months put on, if you will, by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: From time to time, that's correct, yes. I didn't attend all of them, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the purpose of these press conferences?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It varied. Most of the ones that I was invited to were obviously directed to some extent against outside media, international media, but also they discussed domestic events. And the very first one I attended, in fact, was primarily domestic events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when you first met Mr. Kordic, and when you saw him in connection with these press conferences, did you come to any assessments, reach any opinions as to what he was, in terms of a person to deal with and interact with?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: By necessity, that's to some extent subjective, but my impression was that he was extremely capable, and had an impact on the people around him, and was a major player. I didn't see much sign of a sense of humour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Court a little better feel for the kind of things, the actual observations you made that caused you to come to those conclusions? What did you see happening, or hear in front of you, that caused you to come to some of those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Dario Kordic had a very aggressive way of speaking when he was speaking before the media, quite a harsh tone. The people around him seemed to look at him with a mixture of respect -- not always based upon liking the guy -- there was a certain atmosphere around him. And again, this is very subjective: the whole demeanour, the eyes, made you believe that this was a person who was quite passionate about what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it correct, sir, that at about the end of October, 1992, there began to be a series of informal meetings, which were located at the Sarajevo Airport, involving three factions in Bosnia, that is, the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and that the purpose of these meetings was to provide essentially a forum for these groups to discuss issues among themselves?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. It began very informally, and then a sort of evolution or momentum took over and they became progressively more formal as the situation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, was it the case that it was the view of UNPROFOR that these meetings were sufficiently successful that they were more formalised into something that came to be called the Mixed Military Working Group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This group continued to meet from time to time at the Sarajevo Airport?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct, and in fact it became, at one stage, the only means by which the various sides and the United Nations were talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why the Sarajevo Airport?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There were several reasons for that. Again, part of it was evolutionary, in that if I can call them all three sides, although that's an oversimplification perhaps, they were all relatively close to the airport and therefore could meet there, but also, of course, because the airport was kept open most of the time, external prominent people like, for instance, Lord Owen, could actually reach the airport, irrespective of the ground situation across the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you may have mentioned a moment ago, is it fair to say that these meetings for a time were really the principal means or certainly one of the principal means for keeping the three groups talking and trying to stop the hostilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the direct [realtime transcription read in error "correct"] level, that's true, yeah. I actually said "at the direct level", not "at the correct level".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Your Honour, Mr. Nice reminds me to mention to the Court the witness does not, as has been the past practice, does not have a copy of the outline that's been provided to counsel and the Court. He has, in the course of reviewing his testimony yesterday evening, he has a copy of his statement, and if that presents a problem for anyone, that can certainly be retrieved from him. But I wanted to make it clear that there was no mystery or problem, that he did take a copy of his prior interview statement with him to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We don't have a problem with Mr. Pinder reading from his statement, if he wishes. But I just wanted to point out to the Court that we received this 15-page document about five minutes before the proceedings started today. I thought we had an agreement that we would be served with these at least 24 hours in advance, especially with a witness like this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with that after the witness has given evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, is it correct that in your capacity as head of public affairs, you attended almost all of the meetings of the Mixed Military Working Group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't a direct player in it, that wasn't part of my role, but I was an observer at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that these meetings were normally attended by high-ranking military commanders of the three groups and also the representatives of UNPROFOR, and that these meetings dealt primarily with military issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just to put some time frames on these meetings we're going to talk about in the next few minutes, the particular meetings that you were involved in started in approximately perhaps late October or so, as they became more formalised, and continued up until approximately the time that you left in early March of '93; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: From my point of view, yes, but obviously they continued after I had left as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this series of meetings, is it correct to say that the usual representatives of the Serbs was General Gvero, who was a subordinate of General Ratko Mladic, and is it also true that on some occasions, General Mladic personally attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a similar fashion, is it correct that the usual representatives of the Croats was Colonel Blaskic, who was the commander of the HVO Central Bosnia Operative Zone and, as time went by, also Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I must object to the leading nature of that, Your Honour. Insofar as it deals with our client, I think that we need to deal with these matters in the most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter that's in dispute, as to whether he attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, it's not in dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then he can lead, if it's not in dispute. But if there's a dispute about the contents of the meetings, then of course he can't. Mr. Scott, don't lead, please, about the contents of the meeting as far as they relate to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Pinder, that another person who came from time to time, representing the Croat parties, if you will, was General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct, but very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then finally as to the Bosnian Muslim group, the primary representative was Colonel Shiber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your experience that it often happened that the military officers involved in the meetings, in these Mixed Military Working Group meetings, would have to go back and meet with their superiors before agreements could be reached or finalised, or at other times that the particularly important meetings would be attended by more-senior officials?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. It was very often said that they could only take back to their respective masters what was being discussed or proposed. That may have been true; at other times it may have been a tactic. We weren't in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court that as time went by, in terms of the Croat representatives, did you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is where you stop leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, could you tell the Court about Mr. Kordic's role at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: As I had said earlier, initially the meetings were attended by Colonel Blaskic. When the meetings became more formalised and there was a prospect of actually reaching agreements that were going to be signed by the various parties and the level of decision making therefore became perhaps more critical, Colonel Blaskic was replaced and at times accompanied by Dario Kordic. On those occasions when both were together, it was Dario Kordic who took the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, in terms of your last answer, did that continue to be the case at these meetings, except in the instances when General Petkovic would attend?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to any conclusions or make any observations of any differences that you observed between the two men, Colonel Kordic and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They were two different characters, but on those occasions when the two were together at the Mixed Military Working Group meetings, Colonel Blaskic at no time that I saw attempted to cause difficulties or to contradict Dario Kordic. However -- and again what I've mentioned is slightly subjective -- there were times when the body language suggested that Colonel Blaskic did not always agree with what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how Mr. Kordic presented himself at these meetings in terms of his physical attire, the way he held himself out to the participants?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At these meetings, he attended in uniform, and on those occasions when he was addressed as "Pukovnik", which I take to understand as "Colonel", he responded to that address.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of these other groups attending the meetings, the Serbs, the Muslims, perhaps any others, how did they, again in your observation, how did they perceive and react to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I never perceived anything that suggested they felt he shouldn't be there or that he was being incorrectly addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did they address him by any particular title or term?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They certainly used the term "Pukovnik".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, getting into a series of these specific meetings, is it correct, Mr. Pinder, that by November of 1992, the Bosnian Croats and the Muslims still appeared to be allied against the Serbs, although, can you tell the Court did you observe any increasing, or what you perceived to be growing problems or tensions between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There had always been tensions between them, but as the meetings developed, the HVO delegation constantly strove to show themselves as the more mature and statesman-like, at times taking a mediation role. But as time went on, this became even more pronounced so that at times they actually ignored the presidency delegation and spoke directly with the Serbian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on that point that you just mentioned, when you refer to the presidency, can you say a little more, for the record and for the Court, what group or interest was that identified with?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We were very keen, not always with success, to demonstrate, at least to the outside world, that this was not a straight three-cornered fight, it was more complex than that, and we went to great lengths to always refer to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the presidency to try to demonstrate that this was not just, as was often perceived, a Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, can you tell the Court what ethnic group the person General Shiber or Colonel Shiber --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Shiber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Shiber, excuse me, yes, who represented the presidency or represented the -- yes, represented the presidency, what ethnic group he was from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Colonel Shiber was a Croat, a Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to direct your attention to a meeting of the Mixed Military Working Group on the 12th of December, 1992. Do you recall the particular events of that meeting or, basically, the agenda, what happened there, who the participants were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Unless I can refer to my notes, I can't speak particularly about that meeting from memory now. Is that permitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When were the notes made, Mr. Pinder? When did you make the notes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: When I gave my statement two months ago or two or three months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to referring to the notes? It's not a memory game.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand it's not a memory game, Your Honour, but we have received some notes in accompaniment to the statement that Mr. Pinder gave two months ago. I don't know whether those are the notes to which he's now referring. The notes that were attached to the statement that we received appear to be notes that were made contemporaneously when he was in attendance at the Mixed Military Working Group meetings for a number of dates between December 12th, 1992, and December the 22nd, a ten-day period, 1992. Those appear to be contemporaneous. But if he's referring to notes that we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please? Could the counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are a combination. There are notes attached to his statement, which are the most relevant excerpts of the notes that refer to these particular meetings, and when the interview statement was made, they were attached to that statement and they were provided to Defence counsel. It is not every note that he ever took, but it is notes that relates to his statement, describing these particular meetings. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, refer to your notes, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's very kind, thank you. They were notes taken at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In reference, then, back to the 12th of December, 1992 meeting, if you have references there that will remind you, who were the participants for the various groups at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: This was the one that was attended by Lord Owen. The Bosnian Serb delegation was General Gvero, for the HVO Colonel Kordic, and for the Bosnian presidency, as normal, General Shiber. Brigadier Cordy-Simpson was also there, as were the various members of the small group from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As to General Gvero, representing the Serbs, did he have some concerns that the agenda for that meeting, in his view, was too complicated and that the meeting should focus on only two issues, those being the cessation of hostilities and increased freedom of movement for civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. It was felt trying to achieve too much too early from his point of view would be too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how Mr. Kordic or Colonel Kordic held himself out or announced himself at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He announced himself as the representative of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did he provide his own personal statement or assessment, if you will, of the progress of meetings up to that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He formally greeted Lord Owen and said he was grateful for the contribution to the peace process, and he said that the meeting progress was good and asked the other sides to join the HVO in acknowledging the goodwill expressed at the last meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did he display or state any particular position toward General Gvero's concerns about the agenda?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He stressed that the military were servants of the politicians and that he supported the general points put forward by Brigadier Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that Lord Owen participated personally in this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that Lord Owen addressed the meeting and said that he and Mr. Cyrus Vance attached great importance to the Mixed Military Working Group meetings, was glad to hear of the progress being made, he insisted that the four most important points, including the withdrawal of heavy weapons from around Sarajevo and civilian freedom of movement, should be included in one agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. The very reason for Lord Owen's presence was, in fact, that the Mixed Military Working Group was making progress and they were very excited and saw this as the catalyst for further movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a reference here to four points or four important points. Can you relate to the Court, as best you recall, what the four key points that were being discussed at that particular time were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: These were the four points that the agreement that we hoped to bring in were based upon. One was cessation of hostilities, removal of all heavy weapons. I can't remember the exact order of the other two, but it was freedom of movement of civilians and trying to get the civilian power, infrastructure, and communications up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with the discussions around those four issues, do you recall anything further that Colonel Kordic stated about his position or the Croat position on these issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't think I quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In connection with the four issues or four points that you just related, do you recall, in the course of that meeting, whether Colonel Kordic expressed any other views as to the Croat positions on those four issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He said that they agreed to all four points and would be willing to sign immediately on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with the freedom of movement for civilians, can you relate to the Court whether, in some days around this meeting, there had been an agreement or at least a tentative agreement about providing three corridors of access into and out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: This was actually one of the reasons that got the Mixed Military Working Group going on a practical footing. We had been trying to get some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please? --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: From Sarajevo, and three groups had been worked out in some detail on the map. That had been provisionally agreed but had not yet been formalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, you don't have your head set on, since we're all speaking primarily in English at the moment, but the interpreter has asked if you can slow down your testimony a bit for purposes of translation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I understand. Would you like me to wear the head set?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You will get instructions occasionally, perhaps. Now, directing your attention to the next meeting, there was a meeting sometime between the 12th and the -- the meeting on the 12th that you just mentioned and another meeting on the 17th of December, which we'll get to in a moment, and can you tell the Court who the principal participants in this meeting, that meeting, were, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Again, they were General Gvero, Colonel Kordic and Colonel Shiber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, and again can you just give us a general synopsis, if you will, of what took place at that meeting, in terms of what happened at the last meeting and then the continuation of the discussions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The meetings had started to take on a sort of routine where the various sides would try to open with a statement of some sort. General Gvero opened that particular meeting with a statement that primarily was wanting to know why Lord Owen wasn't actually present. To the best of my recollection, Colonel Kordic did not make a statement but said that the delegates had agreed to consult their political masters. He said he had done that and that the HVO absolutely supported the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he make any more specific reference to the people that he particularly had consulted with?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, he didn't name anyone, but said the HVO military top level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the position of -- well, I think there's no dispute, probably, here: Is it correct that Colonel Shiber stated that the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina also agreed to the four-point plan?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court whether Colonel Kordic made any statement about additional approvals or authorisations that he would have to receive to make this agreement absolutely final or binding?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He made, as he very often did, reference to Herceg-Bosna as the supreme body to examine them from the Croatian side, but also said that the HVO were not only ready to announce an end to the hostilities and would respect it, they were ready to make it in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that Colonel Shiber said that he also supported Brigadier Cordy-Simpson's position, and that in his view, an agreement on moving the heavy weapons out of range of Sarajevo would be enough to secure an agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Removal of the heavy weapons was and continued to be one of the sticking points to any agreement. It was considered essential, certainly by ourselves and the presidency, that heavy weapons should be moved back out of range of bombarding Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, then, to the next meeting, on the 17th of December, 1992, unless there is a dispute. Is it correct that the principal participants at that meeting for the Serbs were General Ratko Mladic, and Colonel Kordic for the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. The presidency forces had difficulty getting there because of local conditions within the Sarajevo perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that for UNPROFOR, the principal participants or representatives were General Morillon and Brigadier Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court -- I take it that General Morillon was not one of the people who attended these meetings on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not on a regular basis, no. It was thought best to leave these to Brigadier Cordy-Simpson, as we were actually talking about military matters and were anxious to show that we were not trying to usurp the political process. General Morillon did have a more political role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall and can you tell the Court why General Morillon appeared at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It was because it was hoped that at this meeting, the agreement to end the war and to have movement of civilians returned might be agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether there was any recognition of any connection or linkage, if you will, between the discussions that the Mixed Military Working Group in Sarajevo and the -- if I can use the word "larger" -- peace discussions that were taking place in Geneva at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There was certainly a very real connection, in that we reported progress or lack of it on a daily basis, but also it was seen that this was the interface at which movement was being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that one of the things that General Morillon expressed particular concern about was, in terms of civilian movement, that the roads in Central Bosnia at that time were principally controlled by the Serbs and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Essentially, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you relate to the Court any comments or suggestions that Colonel Kordic made in reference to those matters or about the corridors to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Colonel Kordic was very supportive, to the extent that he proposed mixed checkpoints with HVO forces, to best of my recollection, police, and UNPROFOR, and was quite happy -- in fact, seemed enthusiastic -- to have that cooperative checkpoint system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you also relate to the Court, had there been discussion around this time about evacuating some 1.500 civilians from Sarajevo, if possible, before Christmas?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. That had been one of the supporting moves that we felt would get things going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall whether Colonel Kordic made a reference to that plan at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He was particularly keen to know what had happened to it, as although it had been provisionally agreed, nothing further had been heard on it. The idea had been to do this before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it accurate that General Morillon responded that it had been discussed with the BiH -- that is, the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency -- that the first convoy would be Croats and that it would take place before New Year's Eve?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct, and that the Red Cross would organise it, not UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serb representatives at the meeting had stated that Mr. Karadzic had agreed to the three corridors but wanted to be sure that they would not be abused to move military equipment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is also correct. There was great suspicion on all sides as to the other sides' motives, and there was a concern -- perhaps justified -- that military equipment and reinforcements would be moved around through these corridors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Colonel Kordic made any reference in these discussions to international law and whether -- anything in connection with possible military abuses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He made the point that according to international law, once cessation of hostilities had been signed, it was deemed to have begun, and that the ceasefire should exist throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were not altogether happy with the very simplified form of demilitarised corridors, mainly on the basis of terrain and communications, that in some areas only one road existed, and therefore, if it were to be barred to military vehicles, it would create a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was part of the concept with these corridors that along the corridors, there would be something like a one-kilometre-wide demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was being proposed, again, because of the mutual suspicion of all sides. However, again, because of terrain, the communication difficulties, that would have meant effectively barring certain roads to any form of military movement at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall again whether Colonel Kordic had any specific reaction or response to the question of the one-kilometre-wide demilitarised zones?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He said it hadn't been in the earlier suggestions, and I specifically remember he said as a soldier, he said that all these roads would be very difficult to control because of people living there and the realities of trying to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in this particular meeting, did you see any evidence that, as you testified earlier this morning, that in fact the Croat party and the Serb parties seemed to be increasingly working directly together, to the exclusion of the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: This was a process that had been evolving, again, over some time. There had been instances where the Serb delegation and the HVO delegation would actually go away, normally during the breaks, and pore over a map together, at times excluding the presidency. On this particular meeting, it was so pronounced that one of the presidency representatives was so annoyed he made the point that he insisted on being recognised as the representative of the whole army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this -- the individual you just mentioned, was this Mr. Verschinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Verschinkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Verschinkovic; excuse me. And was there any particular -- when he stated this position or made the presidency's position known, was there any reaction from Colonel Kordic or the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Again, it's slightly subjective, but it was faintly amused that they had caused this reaction. I made an observation at the time that the HVO delegates were enjoying their role as the power brokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say -- I'm not sure, I'm looking at the transcript -- when you say "amused," who acted amused?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention, then, to the meeting on the 20th of December, 1992, is it correct to say that the principal representatives at that meeting of the Mixed Military Working Group was, again, Colonel Kordic for the Croats, General Gvero for the Serbs, and Colonel Shiber for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that on this particular occasion, Graham Masservy-Whiting attended the meeting as Lord Owen's personal representative?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Graham Masservy-Whiting was one of the principal assistants to Lord Owen, and on this particular occasion, because he was in Sarajevo, he attended the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that at this particular meeting, the Serbs presented a paper they had prepared on a number of issues, including freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you relate to the Court whether you recall Colonel Kordic having any particular reaction or response to the Serb proposal?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He said he had consulted military political authorities and he had no remarks to make from their side, but he was keen that hostilities should be stopped and that all parties should take the concrete steps proposed by Brigadier Cordy-Simpson to show that they were really achieving something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Going on to the 21st of December of 1992, were the principal, again, representatives at that meeting Colonel Kordic for the Croats, General Gvero for the Serbs, and Colonel Shiber for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on his arrival at that meeting, or as the meeting started, can you relate to the Court any particular statement or announcement that Colonel Kordic made about his position or authority?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He announced at the very start that he was the representative of the Croatian Council and defence delegation. It wasn't immediately significant to us as to why he had said that, but it became more obvious during the course of the meeting, as they were able to get round the map and actually agree on the spot where the various lines of separation and military positions should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of that meeting, can you tell the Court, did Mr. Kordic have to defer or delay the meeting to seek any other approvals or authorisations from any other Croat authority?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No. That was where the significance of what he had said became apparent. He appeared to be able to take those decisions on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, just pause a moment; I want to make a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, I'll also take advantage of the break to say that again, I think we're both getting some requests to slow down a bit for the translation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I apologise. I haven't forgotten sufficiently that I was an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think I'm more the offender than you. Now, going on to this same meeting, did you have any -- can you relate to the Court any observations that you made in terms of your perception, your visual perception or observations at the meeting, as to any facility that Colonel Kordic displayed in reference to the military matters, the military maps, those sorts of issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Other than the fact that he was obviously well aware of the situation on the ground and understood the military significance of what was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to a meeting on the 22nd of December of 1992. Is it correct that this was a meeting where it was anticipated that a final agreement on a ceasefire, as a culmination of all these preceding meetings, would take place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was the intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on this particular occasion, the senior participant or representative, if you will, for the Croat side was General Petkovic, and the senior representative on the Serb side was General Ratko Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you just relate to the Court, is it fair to say that these two senior officers essentially were there to sign or take advantage of the work that had been done by other representatives of their respective parties?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. The work had been done, obviously, by the previous meetings, and the intention of this meeting had been that the very senior level would set their -- if you like, their seal of approval on what had been negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in these previous meetings, again, the principal representative for the Croats being Colonel Kordic and the principal representative for the Serbs being General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. They had led their respective delegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher, please, to show you Exhibit 331.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I state for the Court and counsel and the witness, Your Honour, there is a package of three exhibits, actually, and for ease of reference, they're attached together in the order in which they will come up in Mr. Pinder's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Pinder?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, from time to time, as the head of public affairs, would you prepare various press statements, or what people might refer to as press releases, for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct. That was an essential part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking to the cover page of Exhibit 331,2, or the first page, in any event, directing your attention in the box to the lower right corner, does that indicate that you had some involvement -- any involvement with this particular documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I was the releasing officer, which meant I gave the authority for it to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the second page, is it fair to say that this was your attempt to publicise some of the developments at the preceding Mixed Military Working Group meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the second paragraph, can you tell the Court whether -- did you -- did you focus on any particular aspects, any particular participants in these prior meetings as to something that you wanted to have publicly presented, if you will?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There were obviously a whole raft of reasons why one drafted press releases. On this particular one, we were trying to emphasise that various sides were working together; and on this particular one, we wanted to give prominence to the fact that it was an HVO initiative that had proposed this scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Moving on, then, from that, are you familiar with the fact, sir, that in approximately January of 1993, a more open armed conflict emerged between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is a matter of record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you relate to the Court whether -- do you recall there being an effort to establish a meeting, on about the 1st of February of 1993, to deal with these issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There were a whole series of attempts to establish meetings, but yes, there was one on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention to Exhibit 422,1. Can you relate to the Court, was there an effort made by UNPROFOR, through the headquarters command in Kiseljak, to invite a senior -- at least one senior representative from both sides; in this case Colonel Kordic for the Croats and General Hadzihasanovic for the Muslim or ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you can tell the Court, looking at Exhibit 422, just by way of explanation, for the record, what these documents relate to or what they essentially constitute?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: If you mean the one I have on the screen, which is the signal --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: -- dated 20th of January, the reason for proposing escorts was that it was considered by both ourselves and the opposing factions extremely unsafe for senior commanders of the factions to risk travelling around, certainly to come to meetings on supposedly neutral territory; therefore we felt that there might be an escort requirement. We wanted to get the people together, of course, who could actually take decisions and get something to change on the ground: i.e., to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was that made the decision as to who to invite to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall, but it would have been either General Morillon or Brigadier Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Cordy-Simpson still the chief of staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the second page of Exhibit 422.1, is that essentially a letter of invitation to Colonel Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct, who was commander of the 3rd Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking to the last page, I'm afraid at the moment I have no particular explanation as to why one is in English and one is in Serbo-Croatian, but is the third page of this document essentially a similar invitation to Colonel Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct. Obviously the actual letters we sent out would normally be, as a matter of courtesy, in the languages of the respective sides. We would always have a translation available to show to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, by this time, had you also heard Mr. Kordic referred to not only as colonel, but as vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I had been aware for some time that he held that office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention back to the first page, the cover sheet, or fax, if you will, paragraph 1, can you confirm for us that the UNPROFOR communication invitation to Mr. Kordic addressed him both in his title as colonel and vice-president?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct. We were also aware that Dario Kordic held command in the immediate Busovaca area in respect of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "held command," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That he was the military commander in the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your work, and being, as you said, part of the inner command, inner group of the UNPROFOR command, did you have any assessment or conclusion -- not only you, but Brigadiers Cordy-Simpson and others -- as to why at this particular time conflict had broken out between the Croat and Muslim sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I had a personal view, and to some extent that would have been supported by the others. I accept that my view may have been slightly more extreme, but the general view accepted was that the conflict had come to a head because of planned negotiations in Geneva on the canton system. I personally felt more strongly about that, because I had been present at a meeting in Sarajevo where those canton lines had been drawn and had made the observation then that I felt, on the ground, such broad lines would create [Realtime transcription read in error "Croat"] problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm looking at my outline because some of the things I think we've already -- in the course of discussion have already been covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to any assessment -- did you --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I interrupt for a second? On the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: -- I did not say, "Such broad lines would Croat problems"; I said "create problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, during this time period, did you continue to interact or see, in various meetings or contexts, both Colonel Kordic and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is right, both formally and informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, did you come to any conclusion or observation of these two in terms of what their reaction was to the strength or effectiveness of the Muslim or Bosnian government army at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There was no doubt that when the 3rd Bosnian Corps started to move, it brought a new dimension to the conflict. Speaking as a professional soldier, they were the first of the indigenous formations I had met who, perhaps in an arrogant way, I would have considered truly professional. They had that impact on the ground, and there is no doubt that both Blaskic and Kordic were both startled and alarmed at both the speed and professionalism of the reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you reach any conclusions or assessments at that time as to who, in connection with those events, appeared to be most in charge on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It seemed to be Dario Kordic who was the more senior of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you relate to the Court, please, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness whether there was anything in particular that indicated that to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There were several things. Part, of course, was related to the Mixed Military Working Group, where whenever the two were together, it had actually been Dario Kordic who had been the senior very openly. But also events on the ground and the odd remark that had been made to me by local officials or civilians indicated that the senior command, whether political or military, rested with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you observe, around or shortly after this time, what you perceived to be a potential conflict, disagreement, between Colonel Kordic and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I never observed a direct disagreement between the two, but there were a number of occasions, particularly when I was talking to Colonel Blaskic, when remarks led me to believe that Colonel Blaskic regarded himself as the professional soldier, and therefore the real expert on military matters, and some dislike of Dario Kordic's handling of the situation. I would also say, and it is subjective, I agree, that there was also some enjoyment of the fact that he, Blaskic, was not ultimately responsible for what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what do you base that on? I anticipate perhaps another question from Judge Robinson. What did you see or hear that would cause you to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That allowing for the somewhat wry and sardonic sense of humour in that part of the world that was prevalent, Colonel Blaskic was enjoying the fact that the situation in the general area was not going well and that he, as I say, was happy that he did not have the ultimate responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it appear to you then, in the next several weeks or while you were still there in Central Bosnia, that this conflict or any of these disagreements appeared to sort themselves out, or did you see anything different develop?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To be honest, it seemed to vary. It was quite difficult to be aware at any one time which of the two might be senior or was most in favour, and by the time I left, as far as I'm aware, officially we didn't know exactly who might be in charge. At the time I left, it did appear to me personally that Colonel Blaskic was coming out of it with more credit than Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say "more credit". Can you explain that further?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: His reputation as a soldier was not being quite so damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you observe, between the two of them, whether there was any direction in which they evolved in particular realms of authority in relationship to each other or in relationship to events?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No. As I say, it was very confused. We were not perfectly informed, of course, and the situation seemed to change from week to week. As far as I'm aware, we had not come to a final conclusion as to who held the ultimate authority at any one time. As near as we could come to it, and again it was an assessment, was that although Colonel Blaskic had authority in the field as a military man, Dario Kordic, possibly because of the mixing of political and military functions, which was not uncommon, held the ultimate authority and held the widest strategic direction of whatever campaign was going on, but it was an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have an assessment whether in any particular localised areas, Colonel Kordic continued to have any particular military or police authority?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It had never been in any contention, as far as we were concerned, that whatever other authority he might have held, Dario Kordic had ultimate authority in the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to a different topic. Can you relate to the Court whether it's correct that in late '92, you saw soldiers in uniform in the Gornji Vakuf area which appeared to you to have some modified HV insignias on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's probably in dispute, so don't lead on it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you observe something about insignias on uniformed soldiers in the Gornji Vakuf area that came to your attention in late '92?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the time, there was considerable disruption in that area, and travelling through that area and to various meetings around Gornji Vakuf, I noticed several soldiers, occasionally even ones who attended the meetings, who had "HV" in embroidered or stamped epaulettes with a Biro'ed "0" put on the end, that this seemed a combination of, to us, rather bizarre and almost naive attempts. I am, of course, not able to say whether these were merely epaulettes that had been provided because of shortage of military uniform and equipment and modified or whether they represented people who were from the HV who had merely changed, in a very childish way, their own existing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say "Biro'ed", or what's the word for how you described the way they were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They were put on with a pen. It was perfectly obvious. It was dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your tenure or tour of duty in Central Bosnia, did you come to any conclusions about the state of the HVO's communication capabilities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: By and large, they were extremely good. Compared to ours, they were excellent. They had mostly control of the telephone networks, and they obviously had military radio communication. I wouldn't say they were perfect, and there were times when those communications may have been cut by hostile action, but by and large, their communications were extremely effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to late '92 or early 1993, can you relate to the Court a particular episode involving a Land-Rover-type vehicle that was owned or used by the ITN news organisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Very well. I was personally involved in it, although I wasn't the only person involved in it. An ITN maroon armoured vehicle used by its reporters and camera teams had been -- I think the term would be "hijacked", certainly taken away from them. It had a heavy machine gun mounted on it and had been used in several incidents around the area. I was asked by the ITN --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say "hijacked", by who or what group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was never completely established, but it was being used by Croatian defence forces subsequently, with a heavy machine gun mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you just continue on with the story, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Attempts went on, I think amounting to over several weeks, to recover that vehicle. Ultimately, it was returned at a meeting which I had with Dario Kordic in his Busovaca headquarters. At the end of that meeting, the vehicle was waiting outside. I then drove it back to Kiseljak and handed it to the ITN authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What caused you to think or to initiate a meeting with Colonel Kordic on the subject?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We had had several attempts, both myself and by the British Battalion, to recover that vehicle, and various people we had spoken to had either said they couldn't do anything about it or that we ought to talk to other people. Ultimately, the process led to Dario Kordic, who was able to secure the return of that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you refer to meeting Colonel Kordic at his headquarters, can you tell us approximately where those headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Over this span of time, I couldn't tell you exactly, but it was a little out of the town, as I drove out of the town, up a hill on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you observe in terms of any troops or armed people that may have been around Colonel Kordic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: As was normal at any headquarters of an authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was an armed presence around it, both outside the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking the witness to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I apologise. I think, psychologically, with headphones on, I start to speak as if I were still a soldier in a tank, and I tend to speak very quickly. I apologise for that. Like all headquarters in that part of the world at the time, it was protected both by soldiers outside the building and inside the building and in the office itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, returning then finally to the part of your duties involved as the head of public affairs in which you had indicated earlier you attended or monitored the press conferences and events in the area, who, over time, did you know to be some of the people who were involved in the press conferences on the Bosnian Croat side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There were a variety of people, but certainly Blaskic and Kordic were very prominent in giving those press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that it was in connection with one of these press conferences, in fact, where you first learned that Mr. Kordic was one of the vice-presidents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: As I said, Colonel Blaskic invited and took me to one of those conferences. It was at that conference that I was introduced to Dario Kordic, and he was introduced to me as the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, was there a particular press conference involving Mr. Kordic that came to your attention around the 1st of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not immediately, but we got reports of it mainly from western journalists, and subsequently I was able to speak to other people and get a rather fuller view, although I didn't have at any time a full text of that particular press conference. It did cause some alarm at the time because of the very explosive statements which were used at the end of that by Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would seek to play a video marked as Exhibit 431. I think it's already been given to the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to the video, obviously, Judge May, but this particular document that is attached as a purported translation, Document Z431A, has been the subject of discussions between myself and the Prosecution, specifically Mr. Nice. Several translations of this particular press conference have been provided to us by the Prosecution. This is one of them. We have put a list of stipulations, provisional stipulations, and objections together and delivered them to the Prosecution covering all of the core documents. A rather extensive exercise, as you can imagine. This is one of the documents that we have challenged and objected to as an inaccurate translation of what was said at the press conference. We don't object to the second translation, but we certainly object to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, is the sensible course to play the video for the moment, we will have the best translation we have, and we will note that it's in dispute and the matter must be resolved in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've double-checked the translations ourselves, obviously, but we recognise they take a different position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with that in due course. We'll have the video first and the best translation you've got. Where is the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It had been attached to the set of exhibits, I hope. The last attachment in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 431A. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the booth can proceed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It improves in a moment, Your Honour. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) Today, as we are talking, General Morillon is holding a meeting in Vitez with two supreme commanders for Central Bosnia, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, HVO commander of the operations area in Central Bosnia and war criminal, commander of the 3rd Muslim Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic. The HVO is asking that the ceasefire agreements signed two days ago be complied with, the roads for humanitarian convoys opened, as it has already been agreed. The HVO is asking that telephone lines for Busovaca which Zenica local authorities have disconnected be reconnected, that power be turned on. I'm certain that our side will be cooperative, and our men have been ordered not to fire a single bullet. Furthermore, we will not return fire if our positions are shelled. Should there be infantry attacks, we will certainly defend ourselves. However, I have to express my personal suspicions regarding the Muslim side. I am not certain that the Muslim forces will not attempt to play the same scenario. They seem to have chosen the war option, having refused the negotiations in Geneva under the given conditions. They want to seize as much territory as possible, to the detriment of the Croat population, because they realise they failed to seize territory from the Serb aggressor. They believe it is easier with the Croats and it is possible to do. But to their deep regret, I once again warn the Muslim people, do not play with fire. If you attack other municipalities, not only that there will be no Bosnia-Herzegovina, there will be no Muslim people left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just give us some more information about this press conference. When is it said to have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was shuffling papers. I apologise. The press conference, to the best of our knowledge, took place on the 1st of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, it was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the tape comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was provided by -- to us, Your Honour, it was provided by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, so we've got the outline of the dispute, I mean first of all is there any dispute that it does represent the press conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that there was obviously a press conference, Your Honour. The particular objection that we have concerns the very last sentence of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have a translation, and we believe it to be the correct translation provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution, which says not "do not play with fire," but "do not play with it," and we believe that to be the accurate translation. This, obviously, is both literally and metaphorically more inflammatory than the other translation which the Office of the Prosecution has provided to us. I don't have my two big binders of the core documents with me. I didn't realise that this was going to be an exhibit. We've received no prior notice of that. But if I had access to that document, Your Honour, I believe in one single set of exhibits there were the two translations, and you could see for yourself the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we have methods here of resolving disputes about translations such as this. It's certainly occurred in other cases. I forget precisely what's done. We'll find out and we'll resolve it. Meanwhile, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we conclude, I apologise, my associates are reminding me there is one additional document which I think we can finish very quickly, if possible. I can do it before or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to hand you what's been marked as Exhibit Z297.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, do you have Exhibit 297 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this is titled "Report On The Ninth Mixed Military Working Group Meeting". By way of explanation of the document, the reference to the "Ninth", is that a reference to this was the ninth in a series of meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you participated in the particular meeting on the 28th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't remember or -- I'm sorry, my question wasn't very good. Do you remember whether you were there or you don't remember one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember if I was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Referring to the item 3, "Participants", would those be the people that you expected during this time period who would have participated in such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I could only say that they were the normal people for a routine meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to paragraph 5 below the opening. Well, before I ask you the next question, whether or not you were at a particular meeting, was it the normal course of business that you would review the minutes of each of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would normally be present when the discussions took place afterwards, because those invariably took place back at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again going back to paragraph numbered 5, do you recall there being a particular item of business or something that was noteworthy on that particular day concerning Colonel Kordic's appearance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't recall this particular incident, but neither do I recall that I was not informed that Colonel Kordic had introduced himself as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your testimony here is that in the course of the fall of 1992, Mr. Kordic, if you will, came on the scene as the senior representative?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
