utterances.text: I think I've already said that that was the case, and when Kordic and Blaskic appeared together, it was obvious that Kordic was the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sayers, you've got the rest of the day, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would anticipate, Your Honour, that I would take approximately three hours with this witness; I hope considerably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To clear up one matter, we've actually located the documents that I was referring to. Let me give you the core bundle reference. Page 5491 is the English translation, and we actually have the Croatian, the original Croatian here, at page 5504. And if I may, I'd just like to have a slight translation of the phrase that I've pointed out. I believe that the Croatian for "fire" is "vatra," and that word does not appear here. I'd just ask the usher ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I guess that it's only this sentence which is in dispute in the translation, or is there any other thing in this ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, there are a couple of other things that are in dispute, Your Honour. First of all, this document, page 5491 of the core bundle, says that the conference occurred in the middle of February, 1991, not the 1st of February. And there are some relatively significant deviations from the version that has been presented to the Trial Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: But the translation problem you have is with the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This specific translation problem, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have asked the registry to look into this, and we'll get it resolved one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, my name is Steve Sayers, and I represent Dario Kordic. I'm going to ask you a series of questions. If any of them are unclear or you don't understand them, just tell me, and I will rephrase them, because it's important to get an accurate transcript here. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you arrived in Central Bosnia in mid-October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you started to work in the UNPROFOR headquarters, working for the staff of Brigadier General Roderick Cordy-Simpson in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you worked as the head of the public affairs for UNPROFOR, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the headquarters in Kiseljak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many people worked for you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It varied and built up as time went on. Initially a very small group, perhaps about four; ultimately, nearer 15.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we ask the counsel to please speak closer to the microphone for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When did you first speak with representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Pinder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters were asking for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The interpreters were asking for me to stand closer to the microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you have in mind, Mr. Sayers, the interpreters when you're asking the questions; and Mr. Pinder, if you could bear in mind to leave a gap after the question so it can be interpreted before you reply --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It makes life slightly more difficult, but it is much easier for those having to interpret.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: My apologies. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think we are both equally --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Reprimanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, when did you first speak with representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Pinder?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the term. I was interviewed, I think, in May, early May, back in the U.K., by someone I understood to be one of the investigators. Am I allowed to say the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Carry Spork.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that resulted in a statement that was dated May the 29th through May the 31st, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So do I take it that you actually met with representatives of the Prosecution during those three days, and not in early May?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think I was originally approached in early May, but it was actually over the bank holiday period that the actual interview took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On May the 29th, 30th, and 31st?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: If that was the bank holiday weekend, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two months ago?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you have your notes with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You didn't make copies of all of your notes available to the Prosecution, did you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just selected snippets of them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you left Central Bosnia at the beginning of March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you were in the theatre, if you like, for a grand total of about five months?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to ask you a few questions about your background, training, and experience, sir, did you receive any higher education after leaving grammar school in Yorkshire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I didn't go to university, if that's what you mean, but I did subsequently earn two degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: One from the equivalent of the civil service foreign office, interpreter exam, and the final diploma of the Institute of Linguists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was the subject that you studied there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: German.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you speak Croatian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you had any political training at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Political training in the sense that I was trained and qualified as a staff officer, and of course, when I took over the job of chief of public information for NATO in northern Germany, I did the NATO press officers' course, which included political training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you were in Central Bosnia, was your rank major?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How long had you held that rank?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would have to think about that. I would think close on eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What is the Council for Education in World Citizenship?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It's an independent educational charity formed in 1939, originally by those people who went on to form both the League of Nations and UNESCO, and its primary role today is to try and produce material and seminars and events, including Internet work, for young people around the world to understand other cultures, and hopefully, through that, find a more peaceful way of coexisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your job as head of public affairs involved setting up a press centre, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And a system for informing the international press of things that were going on in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was the aim, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your job required you, therefore, to liaise with journalists; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the press systems of various countries, too?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And to the extent possible, you were also required to liaise with local media; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And local public officials?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that you set yourself the task of gaining a comprehensive understanding of the political and military situation in Central Bosnia when you first took up your job?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was what we set out to do, yes. We were, of course, thrown in at the deep end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What did you learn about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? What was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's quite difficult to answer in several sentences. They were possibly -- and this is obviously a generalisation -- or seemed to be the more sophisticated of the various communities, and by that I mean, I suppose, subjectively, westernised; not to suggest the others were not, but they seemed more at home with the western concepts. They seemed to have more people who understood the larger dimensions of what the implications might be of the conflict there. They were -- perhaps they would say, with justice -- completely paranoid about the so-called Muslims and what would happen if the Muslim government, as they frequently called it, took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the massacre that occurred at the villages of Dusina and Lasva on the 26th and 27th of January, shortly before the press conference that concluded your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can say nothing direct. I wasn't present, nor did I visit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that in fact numerous civilians had been shot to death?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mrs. Zeljka Rajic's husband had been shot to death with about a dozen bullets and had the heart cut out of his body?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: You may not like me for saying this, but I have long since stopped being shocked by what human beings do to each other, and I was not aware directly of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It's a long time ago. I think it was Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many vice-presidents were there of that entity?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: More than one. I can't remember at this stage how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What were the functions of the office of vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this distance, I can't remember. I would have known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can't tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Of course not. It's seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what the HDZ BiH was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: HDZ -- there were a whole range of abbreviations used to describe various parties. I think the HDZ was the Croatian Community in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the national president of that political party was during the time that you were in charge of press affairs for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No longer. I repeat, it's seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the local president was in Kiseljak, where you were based, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would have known at the time. I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: As I say, I would have known at the time. I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you know it was not Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please space out questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't know now; I would have known then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you can't tell the Trial Chamber whether, for example, Mr. Kordic held any position in the HDZ BiH in Busovaca -- or Kiseljak, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I know from memory that he held the equivalent of what we would have called garrison commander of the local defence forces in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And where did you derive that information from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: From information we had at the time. It wasn't contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever consult military information summaries regarding the chain of command in the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the time, I would have done indirectly, but that wasn't my direct mission. That would have been done by the information section. There was confusion, always, in the U.N., because they used the word "information" for what I, as a military officer, would have used as "intelligence." I wasn't involved in intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the name of the military brigade of the HVO that was stationed in Busovaca was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does the brigade Brigada Nikola Subic Zrinjski sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just show the witness a milinfosum, Your Honour, it basically summarises the HVO chain of command in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D49/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention, if I may, to page 2. In the HVO Central Bosnia Operative Zone, the commander is identified as Tihomir Blaskic; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: This is paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you could just move the -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for the HDZ, Dario Kordic is identified as a significant person?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held in the HDZ? I think you've already said that you do not.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think -- I think that's correct, and I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you could just turn to the next page, please. In the Second Operative Zone group, reporting to Colonel Blaskic, was the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet, but let's look. Which paragraph is that under?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Forgive; me, I haven't actually found that yet. Could you give me the name again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right at the top of the screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Subic Zrinjski?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. I misheard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What's the name of the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Niko Jozinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet commander Niko Jozinovic of the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade based in Busovaca, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall that I did. I do recall once meeting Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's what it says he is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning back to the HDZ, do you know how many vice-presidents there were of this political party, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think I've already said that. At this stage, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if I suggested to you that there are five vice-presidents, and that Mr. Kordic was one of them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the HVO was, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The HVO was the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was a military organisation, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Primarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of the HVO was at the time of your tour through Central Bosnia, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall at this stage, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll just show you a document, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D50/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My colleague tells me, Your Honour, that we apparently do not have a number for the previous document, the milinfosum number 98 -- oh, it was 49/1? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, what's the point of showing the witness this document unless he's actually seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just want to see if it jogs his memory, Your Honour, as to who the president of the HVO was. Just turn to the last page, Your Honour, and Mr. Pinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I have recollection of the name; I quite honestly wouldn't recall that he was president of the HVO HZ -- HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Zoran Maric?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The name is not familiar at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know that he was the president of the HVO in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall that there was a change in command of the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, no, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever met commander Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that he was actually appointed as the commander of the Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade, and that he replaced commander Niko Jozinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't know that. I notice, though, that some of these materials are from one battalion group in the UNPROFOR zone. I was responsible for the areas of eight battalions, and therefore I wouldn't necessarily have known the day-to-day transitions in each area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would concede, therefore, that the regiment that was actually stationed in the area which had responsibility for Busovaca would know more, much more, about the military chain of command and the civil chain of command, than you did?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: In that particular area, we could expect them to know and to provide us with information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just show you the next milinfosum, if I may, dated February the 26th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D51/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pinder, I do not need to detain you too long with this document. This is a milinfosum prepared by the 1st Cheshire Regiment, and I'm sorry that we don't have a better copy. But just as a matter of background, the 1st Cheshire Regiment actually had responsibility for the areas of Vitez and Busovaca, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you see that by this time, in the middle of the page, the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade is now Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that the deputy commander did not change, it was still Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Commander Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know who the chief of staff militarily was for the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the time, I might have done. I don't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic? Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Well, the name obviously does, as I met him several times. But at this distance, I can't recall exactly what his title was, and these titles did change. It was an evolutionary process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But there's no question that on the 22nd of December, 1992, Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic turned up at the Mixed Military Working Group meeting as the military supreme commander of the HVO in all Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's absolutely true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know, sir, how the HVO chain of command was broken down?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To be quite honest, that was one of our difficulties. They seemed to be evolving and our information was not always perfect, nor was it my direct responsibility to know the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question, "No"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The answer is, "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand that the British army or the 1st Cheshire Regiment had its local headquarters in the village of Nova Bila, just outside Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's substantially correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart was the commanding officer of the 1st Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that it would be Lieutenant Colonel Stewart who would be in the best position to give us all insights into the actual HVO command structure and chain of command in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: In his direct area of responsibility, he would know, but he would not know and he did not know the larger picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You say that Colonel Blaskic was the commander of the 1st Operative Zone on page 3 of the statement that I think you've been consulting throughout your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is what I wrote at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that, in fact, Colonel Blaskic was actually the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and that the 1st Operative Zone was one of the levels of command underneath him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would not know at this stage whether that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Mr. Kordic, you say that you first heard of him when you arrived in Central Bosnia and that you heard of him in a political context initially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that he had actually been a journalist before the outbreak of the civil war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I heard various versions of what he had been before. Journalist was one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you arrived in Central Bosnia, there's simply no dispute, and I don't think that you would dispute this, that there was a vicious, bitter, and bloody civil war going on between the various constituent peoples in that country; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation of "civil".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation of "civil". He can talk about what the conflict was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what are you saying? I can't hear. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I'm not speaking very well today. We object to the characterisation of it being a civil war. That's a characterisation by counsel. He can ask just a neutral question about the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's the very point that we're going to have to decide, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was a conflict going on between the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't know that there was a conflict going on between the Serbs in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, sir. You were aware that the Serbs had attacked their Croat and Muslim compatriots, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It was a very complex situation. There were Serbs on both sides, there were Croats on both sides, there were Muslims on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Everyone in the country was fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There was internal conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Amongst the inhabitants of the country; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on. You say that when you first arrived in October of 1992, you heard that Mr. Kordic held, to use your words, a relatively-high position in what the Croats termed Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At first, I only heard that he held a high position. When I was actually introduced to him, I was told that he was a vice-president. I agree with you, I was told "a vice-president". I never assumed there was only one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I mean I think that you just don't know how many vice-presidents there were of HZ-HB --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I had several years as chief executive of chambers of commerce. Sometimes we had six vice-presidents, sometimes we had two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also viewed it as quite a breakthrough, I believe, that you were permitted to attend press conferences that were given by the Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me that at those press conferences that you attended, three, I believe it was, there would first be a briefing on the military situation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be Colonel Blaskic who would give that briefing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Normally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then there would be a presentation followed by Mr. Ignac Kostroman, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Finally, for the political perspective, Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I wouldn't disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you have stated that you do not recall whether you saw Mr. Kordic wearing any kind of a uniform at these press conferences.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I honestly can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know whether Mr. Kordic had a military background at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I never heard that. I know there was national service, but I don't know whether, at this stage, he had done the full service or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know whether he actually held any officer's rank in the JNA, the former Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, no, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever know that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember if I ever knew that. I'm sorry, I'm not being deliberately difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was Colonel Blaskic, I believe, that you said who was the person who first introduced you to Mr. Kordic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He introduced you to "Mr. Kordic", not "Colonel Kordic"; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think that would be correct. Certainly, it's true I didn't have any indication of military rank at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when Mr. Kordic was first introduced to you as a colonel, as having some kind of military rank?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think it was actually on the Mixed Military Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: In the British army, anyway, how do you actually become a colonel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm resisting cynicism and saying that you get promoted through qualifications and experience and commands you've held before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It usually takes an extremely long time to travel up the chain of command, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But, nonetheless, normally --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, there would be a progression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is there any such thing in the British army as an honorary colonel, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, there are, of regiments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little about that? What kind of military function does an honorary colonel have in the regiments in the British army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: With the actual regiments themselves, very little. What function he actually has would determine what he or she might normally do. It is possible, for instance, for a field marshal to be an honorary colonel in a regiment and be chief of the general staff. Equally, Princess Anne is an honorary colonel of several regiments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, but you agree that this is a position that's frequently reserved for, for example, political figures, prominent political figures?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It is normally exclusively denied to political figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the people that are given this title, if you like, they don't actually have the ability to command troops and --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, it's an honorary title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They don't have the ability to give orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not as a result of being an honorary person. But this is a purely peace-time, ceremonial rank. It is not the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're suggesting, and I don't know if this is the suggestion, that Mr. Kordic was an honorary colonel in the same way as a field marshal or somebody of a similar rank is an honorary colonel in Britain, I think you better put that directly to the witness to hear what his reaction is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will get around to that, Your Honour. I think we may as well do it right now. No time like the present, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is as good a time as any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were first introduced to Mr. Kordic as "Colonel Kordic" in the Mixed Military Working Group meetings in December of 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's probably correct. Certainly towards the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You had never heard of him as a colonel before that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Never been introduced to him as a colonel before that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not specifically with rank. However, I would have to put a distinction to say that by that time, we knew that he was responsible for the defence forces around Busovaca, or we believed that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, let's put it -- well, where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: From a variety of sources, and we assessed it, rightly or wrongly -- we may have been wrong -- more in the context of earlier European conflicts where, for instance, the town mayor might have been made local defence commander. But it could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What sources?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, I wouldn't be aware what those sources were, but they would almost certainly have been local sources, which may or may not have been reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Zoran Maric was the mayor of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To get back to Judge May's point, the Mixed Military Working Group, I think you said in your direct examination, and I don't think there's any dispute about it, was the only forum in existence in the December 1992 time period which provided an active dialogue for the three main participants in this internal conflict, the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't agree with your last part of that definition, but I accept that the Mixed Military Working Group was where the various factions were getting together to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. So you had to have a military rank in order to participate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I personally would not have seen that as being necessary, but I can see why it would have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, do you know whether Dario Kordic was in fact formally appointed as a colonel of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never seen any orders of appointment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Any publications which announced that appointment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never seen Dario Kordic sign a military order, I take it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I've never seen him physically sign one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, to turn to a different subject, your superior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, I would like an answer to the question which I posed. Mr. Pinder, if the suggestion was made that the role which Dario Kordic was carrying out when you observed it was similar to that of an honorary colonel in the British army, what would your answer be to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't conceive, in the local situation as it then was, there would have been any reason for people to be honorary colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But to complete the thought, Mr. Pinder, and I think you've already said this, you don't know whether, in fact, Mr. Kordic was actually an HVO colonel, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, to get back to the subject I was about to raise, your superior officer, I take it, was Brigadier Roderick Cordy-Simpson then, now Major General Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Major General Sir Cordy-Simpson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was the principle negotiator representing the British army, anyway, at the Mixed Military Working Group meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He was most definitely not representing the British army. He represented UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But he was a senior ranking British member of the UNPROFOR negotiation team, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He served, I believe, as chief of staff under Lieutenant General Philippe Morillon.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also under Brigadier General Martinez-Coll, as General Morillon's second in command?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So at least on the British side, you would have to concede, would you not, that Major General Cordy-Simpson would be the most knowledgeable about the actual negotiations, what went on at the negotiations that occurred in the Mixed Military Working Group meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken at some length upon your claim that Mr. Kordic or Colonel Kordic, as you have described him, was clearly superior in the chain of command to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That wasn't only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You stated that it would have been obvious to anyone present at the meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It would have been normally obvious, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the earlier meetings that were attended only by Colonel Blaskic, do you recall whether he brought along with him a political commissar at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The term's an interesting one, and it's one we unofficially used as well. Normally, it was Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read to you from the statement that Major General Sir Roderick Cordy-Simpson submitted to the Prosecution. It's on page 6. "Within the HVO, there was evidence of a structure where people, such as the mayor or his military equivalent, sat alongside each other. Dario Kordic was not military but a politician. "For a period, Kordic was the representative of the HVO at the MMWG meetings in the absence of Blaskic, but I am not sure of the relationship between the two or who was superior to the other. Blaskic always seemed to be able to deliver on military decisions, if he wished to, but with Kordic it was more uncertain." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I wouldn't disagree with that, depending on the time it was written, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He also stated that Brigadier General Petkovic was older, a professional soldier, and he was definitely the commander. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would agree, over the whole area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever speak to Lieutenant Colonel Robert A. Stewart regarding his perceptions of Dario Kordic's role within the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We would have discussed that several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true Lieutenant Colonel Stewart told you that he never considered Dario Kordic to be a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just cite to you page 23855 of Colonel Stewart's testimony in Blaskic just a month ago. He said: "Colonel Blaskic was, in my opinion, the real commander of the HVO in Central Bosnia. I never, ever thought that Kordic was the commander. I never, ever referred to Kordic as the commander, or anybody else." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: If he said that, then that's obviously what he believed. I don't think we ever thought Dario Kordic was a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He also elaborated, on page 23871, as follows: "Kordic always spoke in political terms. He always talked, you know, of destiny and, you know, the sort of grand picture. Certainly, the soldiers naturally followed Colonel Blaskic, not Kordic, to whom I gave no rank, because I don't think he had one." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was obviously his opinion. The fact that he was addressed as "Pukovnik" both by his own people and the other negotiating parties as some stage is what I'm basing my assessment on, but of course that is my assessment from the fact that he was called "Pukovnik".

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course, you would have to agree that even between the upper echelons of the command structure in the British forces present in Central Bosnia at the time that you were there, there would be room for disagreement --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- where you're not absolutely sure --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. There's doubt as to the command structure in your mind, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There was certainly doubt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there still is, isn't there, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter that we're going to have to resolve in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to the Mixed Military Working Group meetings that you've described, when did this group first convene?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Again with time, I can't recall exactly when. I thought it would have started an informal process towards the end of October, early November, and it sort of grew. It wasn't planned. There wasn't any great master plan. We were all trying to find our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have been given a copy of some snippets of notes that you prepared when you were in attendance at some of these meetings. I believe that you gave anything that contained any relevance or reference to Mr. Kordic to the Prosecution when they interviewed you two months ago, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The very first one of these notes that we have is dated the 12th of December, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The last meeting that was attended by Mr. Kordic, I believe, was December the 21st.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't know if that was the last meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, why don't you take a look at your notes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They would only record those meetings which I had been asked to discuss, but I'll certainly take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't see anywhere where I say that's the last meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he attend the meeting on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: December 1992.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, because that was the one between what should have been the three generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your notes don't reflect that he ever attended any meetings after December the 21st, 1992; isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's a fact from my notebooks, but neither did I attend every single meeting after that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand. But your notes only show Mr. Kordic in attendance at these meetings over a nine-day period; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: My notes, as such, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say that Mr. Kordic turned up at some of these meetings in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: There was, of course, a lot of wearing of combat kit by people on all sides, whether they were military or not. Some people might have worn a combat jacket, others might have been wearing combat trousers. But on this particular occasion, it was significant to us that this was a proper uniform. It was actually quite a new jacket. I remember there was an HVO slash to it. I don't recall, as I said in my evidence, whether that was on the chest or on the shoulder, but I do recall the patch was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're telling us, I think, that he turned up in camouflage clothing with an HVO patch somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: And the full boots, and the panoply, if you like, of the aides around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Including a rosary bead and a crucifix that he habitually wore; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We noticed that he always wore that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He did not wear any rank insignia that you recall at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, but many of them didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. He didn't have a name tag or a rank slide that said "Pukovnik Kordic", did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you would agree with me that Mr. Kordic, and the Croats generally, acted as mediators during the Mixed Military Working Group meetings held in December of 1992. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That appeared to be the line that they were taking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They liked and, in fact, relished and enjoyed the role as mediators in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I made that observation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mediating between the Muslim or BiH side, on the one hand, and the Serb side, on the other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It was not a benign mediation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But mediation, nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It appeared to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: An attempt to stop conflict rather than ferment it; wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes, but deliberately talking separately to the Serb delegation and excluding the Bosnian presidency was not helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you agree that the matter of maps and cantons and ethnic divisions, things of that variety, were topics of the most vivid and lively conversation amongst all of the political and military figures in Bosnia-Herzegovina in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, the Vance-Owen Plan, I believe, was being actively discussed and thrashed out at that time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those were negotiations occurring in Geneva; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Ultimately in Geneva, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who attended the Geneva negotiations representing the HZ-HB and the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I believe on certain occasions it was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Boban. Anyone else that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall at this distance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know whether Mr. Kordic ever attended any meetings in far-off places like Geneva, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't. But if I can make a point, with your permission, at the time of the Falklands War, I would have known the names of all the Argentinian cabinet and most of their commanders on the ground. I don't know them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to the notes that you prepared for a minute, I believe that you went through them carefully and extracted only the ones that were, to use your words, specifically relevant because of the role that Mr. Kordic was fulfilling at the MMWG meetings.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The books are general. They include orders, groups, my instructions to various people, and of course records of various meetings that took place, and, yes, I extracted those which seemed relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, then, that Mr. Kordic, or Colonel Kordic as you describe him, assumed no significant role in the negotiations before December the 12th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, he didn't turn up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When the time came to actually -- sorry. When the time came actually to sign a written agreement, it wasn't Mr. Kordic that signed the agreement or was prepared to do so, it was Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At the time, that was the intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you don't know whether any peace agreements at all were ever signed by Mr. Kordic, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll go over some of those in just a second. But let me go through each one of these meetings, and I just have a few questions, if I may. I think there were three or four meetings that you discussed specifically. The first one was on December the 12th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Umm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In this meeting, I believe that you say that Mr. Kordic stressed that goodwill should be shown before the Christmas holidays to all; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Especially to children, women, and the elderly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was because the children, women, the elderly, and the other components of the population were expecting some kind of progress in the discussions at the MMWG meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's the point that Mr. Kordic made?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We were all making that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He later emphasised to you that it would have to be political negotiations that would bring an end to the civil war; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you that or he told the participants in the meeting that they should all express better goodwill and work towards the peace process?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was little discussion, if any, of the military intricacies behind the ceasefire proposal, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: On that particular meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But Mr. Kordic turned up and indicated a willingness, on the part of the HVO, to sign any ceasefire agreement and to sign it immediately?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct, but at that time he was styling himself "Colonel Kordic".

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand. But actually the ceasefire agreement that ultimately eventuated from these nine days of negotiations in which he participated was not signed by one side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which side was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mean the BiH presidency, the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of about 30 ceasefires.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether Mr. Kordic signed any of those 30 ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, there was reference to another meeting that occurred sometime between December the 12th and the 17th of 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What date; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't, because in my notes, unfortunately, I didn't actually put anything more than "December" on that particular instance, so it's bracketed between a meeting on the 12th and some facts that I put in of a totally unrelated event on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you didn't provide a copy of that to the Prosecutors, and therefore to us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I certainly provided a copy of that meeting. I merely said I didn't know on which day it took place between the 12th and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's see if we can go over what was said at this meeting. I believe Mr. Kordic told the attendees that he had spoken with the Croat, quote, "political masters"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct. That's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's straight from your notes; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's straight from my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It wasn't said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the political masters told Mr. Kordic that there was complete support at the top for a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you don't know who was at the top, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, at this stage, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic indicated a willingness on behalf of the HVO to freeze all military activity?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that there would be no new deployments of any forces; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But he emphasised nonetheless that Herceg-Bosna was the supreme body to examine these decisions from the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was the point he made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know who in Herceg-Bosna had to do that, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next meeting occurred, I believe, on December the 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct. The next meeting that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. You didn't attend all of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that General Morillon told the attendees that the Muslim side could not be represented, that would be late, because they had been detained at a roadblock?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And General Morillon also emphasised that it would be wise to establish a practical framework for an agreement so that a higher-level process could begin?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those are the words that he used?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you recorded that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with respect to the matter of HVO road blockades, it's true, is it not, that Mr. Kordic said that as to the HVO road blockades, that UNPROFOR could take control of them all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's one comment in your notes, sir, that is rather intriguing. It says, quote, "We have to have professional interpreters," followed by an exclamation mark?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber some insight on why that was important or necessary?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes. If I can explain, I am also a professional interpreter, English/German, and therefore I had some knowledge of the difficulties of trying to interpret. I have been increasingly concerned, and had made those concerns known, and they'd been accepted, that we were actually dealing with very sensitive and complex matters. Whether those belonged in the political or military area didn't matter; the Mixed Military Working Group were the ones discussing them, and we were relying on people who were not, by and large, professional interpreters. They were local. Some were even teachers of English, but there's a great difference between being able to teach and speak a language and being able to interpret it. We were also concerned that, being local, those people could come under pressure to do things or to say things that were not accurate because of, perhaps, where their relatives were. And those were the reasons why we made those representations that we needed fully professional interpreters. It was getting too complex, I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also refer to a comment that was made by a gentleman by the name of Verschinkovic, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in your notes it says, quote, "Presidency lack the mil. expertise to even understand the implications of their plan," unquote.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'll answer it first in a general sense, if I may. One of the concerns we had mainly was that a lot of the people who had got high-level appointments, whether they were military or political, were not actually professionals in their particular field -- and that is in no way to be arrogant; it certainly isn't intended to be -- that they were in an incredibly difficult situation, one that we could only partially relate to, and they were trying to gain experience of high-level diplomatic matters, of trying to talk to each other and establish procedures of which they themselves had no great personal experience. And that was our concern. And one of the ways the Mixed Military Working Group tried to help that was to suggest and bring along a knowledge of how to talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. If we could turn very briefly to the next meeting on December the 20th, 1992, I believe that Mr. Kordic told all of the attendees, and you, that he had consulted the military and political authorities and had actually no remarks to make regarding the pending suggestions from the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct, because they had already agreed to them previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, he urged all parties to agree to the immediate cessation of all hostilities, did he not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he also urged all participants at this meeting to take the concrete step, to use your notes, proposed by Brigadier, then --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Cordy-Simpson, to show that they had achieved something. What was that concrete step?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage I can't remember, but they were obviously the four points, but there had been technical discussions on where particular lines should be drawn, even down to going the left side of particular districts; which roads and junctions should be included in which part. And there were time frames attached to that. Certain things were to be achieved by the 21st of December, by the 23rd, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there's another reference in your notes to Mr. Kordic emphasising that the Christmas celebrations were coming up --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and that this was a good opportunity --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- a perfect opportunity to achieve something?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you find Mr. Kordic to be a religious man, in your experience with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: We had assumed that he had a reason for wearing a crucifix. I have no idea of his religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the next meeting, now. December the 21st, 1992, is the last meeting that you attended -- the last Mixed Military Working Group meeting that you attended -- at which Mr. Kordic spoke; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Sorry, which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: December 21st.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I saw a reference in your notes that say as follows: "LO feels sufficient political progress now made to leave mil. to mil. experts"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that an accurate rendition --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- of what your notes say?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes. "LO" would mean "Liaison Officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it mean "Lord Owen"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It could have done. In that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It did, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah. It probably did, actually, in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever read Lord Owen's book, "A Balkan Odyssey"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I did scan it. I didn't buy a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the name "Dario Kordic" does not appear in this book once?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's a dramatis personae right at the beginning of the book containing maybe a couple of hundred names. Did you know that Dario Kordic's name doesn't appear anywhere in that dramatis personae?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Neither does mine, and I helped Lord Owen on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that made the suggestion that Mr. Kordic should actually turn up to these Mixed Military Working Group meetings in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't. I assumed -- we had all assumed some consultation process had gone on within their own party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just show you one document, I'd like to see if this jogs your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D52/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This actually comes, Your Honour, from the core bundle, page 5582; that is, the Prosecution's core bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd just like to turn your attention to paragraph 4 of Colonel Blaskic's recommendations, where he says, "I propose that our side is represented by deputy president of HZ-HB, Mr. Dario Kordic, and secretary Ignac Kostroman." Did Mr. Blaskic ever relate that suggestion to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have mentioned in your direct testimony a visit down to the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that around the same time, the winter and -- beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It would have been around -- around the turn of the year, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know that a ceasefire order was actually signed on January the 20th, 1993, and that it was signed in the Gornji Vakuf area by Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this distance in time, I don't recall that; but there were frequent ceasefire agreements and signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If I might just show you a document that was attached to milinfosum 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D53/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is virtually illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is indeed, Your Honour, but I'm actually referring to the last two pages of this document, which is perfectly legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This January the 20th, 1993, order: Have you ever seen it? The order that was signed by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and commander of the 4th Corps of the BiH army, Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't say with 100 per cent certainty, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that joint orders had been issued for the cessation of all hostilities in the Gornji Vakuf area on January the 20th, 1993, by the -- at the very -- signed by the highest commanders in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall at this stage the exact date, but I do recall that they were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you attend high-level ceasefire negotiations in Kiseljak on January the 26th, 1993, that were conducted between Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, Colonel Blaskic, and General Merdan, the second in command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I was only sporadically present at those because I was actually running the press centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: -- for the journalists who were interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it's true, is it not, that on January 26th, high-level negotiations occurred between highly-placed military figures aimed at producing a ceasefire in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic didn't attend those negotiations at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, those negotiations actually went on to the very next day, January the 27th, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that meeting, Brigadier General Cordy-Simpson actually brought the negotiators before the TV cameras?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To cement, if you like, the agreement that had been -- or the informal agreement that had been reached there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I organised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. That's your bailiwick, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And he made the negotiators shake hands?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't think he made them, but they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Once again, will you please try to space out questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you get that, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I stand chastised once again, Your Honour. I will do my best to slow down.
