utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Brigadier Cordy-Simpson also made the parties reaffirm their commitment to a ceasefire, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: They did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you know that a ceasefire agreement actually was signed as a result of this meeting that was presided over by Brigadier Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I believe that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember. I would have done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, I actually have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D54/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pinder, is this actually a copy of the ceasefire agreement that was signed on January the 30th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right. It wasn't signed at Kiseljak; it was signed further into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was actually signed at the BritBat headquarters in Nova Bila, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Nova Bila; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On behalf of the HVO, Franjo Nakic signed the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: At this stage, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that he was Colonel Blaskic's second in command, would that sound right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It could well be. I can't say at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it was also signed, on the Muslim side, by Colonel Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's right. I recall Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was actually the second in command to General Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Commander of the 3rd Corps, headquartered in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The document is also signed by Lieutenant Colonel Stewart; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also by Jeremy Fleming from the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who is Jeremy Fleming?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: The ECMM had been taking an increasingly active part in the various negotiations, and in fact had set up a team -- I can't remember where it was based; somewhere between Vitez and Kiseljak -- who were actually monitoring, in a joint task force organisation, the various moves that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At all events, the document, I think we can all see, is not signed by Mr. Kordic at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: You said yourself they are signed by deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that implementing orders, joint orders, were to be one obtained from the commanding officers of the Croat forces and the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I might just ask the usher to show Mr. Pinder a document which has already been identified as defence exhibit D17/1,17.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, you are being shown the signature page only of this agreement. If you actually flip it around, it says, "Joint order from commander, 3 Corps, BiH army, and commander of HVO, Middle Bosnia Operational Zone"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic on behalf of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also signed by General Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's countersigned by Jeremy Fleming, the chairman of the joint commission; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct, yes. This is the one that was setting up the monitoring teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the joint commission was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: This is the group I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll show you the charter of that in just a second, but before I do, let me show you another document, which is a series of implementing orders signed by the joint commanders of the HVO and ABiH forces.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D55/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pinder, I think there's a linkage between these two exhibits. In fact, the first order contained in exhibit D17/1,17 is that joint orders signed by both commanders are to be confirmed with -- the following orders are hereby issued. And then there are a number of different orders. If you would take a look at the exhibit that's just been put before you, would you agree with me that those are in fact the implementing orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Regarding a variety of things, they're pretty self-explanatory, and there's really no need to go over them. But you would agree with me that each one of these orders is signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, commander of the Middle Bosnia HVO Operative Zone, and by General Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: As a former soldier, I would say these represented field army orders for the field army commanders, not necessarily the commanders of the armed forces. But yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But they are signed by the commanders of the forces in the area, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Of the field forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you mentioned the joint commission. Are you referring to something that was initially known as the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That, I think, is what it progressed from yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the commission actually moved from Busovaca to Vitez in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I had forgotten that, but it could well be. I think I said I didn't know exactly where it had been located all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could just ask the usher to show Mr. Pinder an exhibit that's already been marked as exhibit D23/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the document that's just been put on the ELMO? And I believe it may be on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And although I can't recall it word for word, yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is an agreement that -- it's entitled "Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission Charter"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the whole aim of this body was to monitor and record the situation in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Kordic was not a member of the joint coordination commission at all, was he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, he wasn't, but I don't quite understand the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, let's see. The joint coordination commission, to monitor activities in the entire Busovaca area, consisted of a committee; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that committee consisted of the following. First, the commanding officer of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Stewart; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Second, the ECMM chairman, which is --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Jeremy Fleming? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Third, the commander of the BiH 3rd Corps, which was General Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And fourth, the commander of the HVO central command, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in turn, there was a subordinate body?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Consisting of the ECMM chairman, who we've just identified?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The chief of staff of the joint commission; do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A BritFor major; do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember at this stage. I'd remember the name if you told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the BiH 3rd Corps; that was --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Colonel Dzemal Merdan, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, finally, the deputy commander of the HVO central command, who would be Colonel Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. 15 Indeed, both sides of the signatories to this ceasefire agreement on January 30th, 1993, agreed to broadcast this agreement to the local media, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you assist in this regard since that was your bailiwick?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I didn't generally assist in that, but of course BritBat had their own public information establishment, as did the other battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact Mr. Kordic did not appear at that conference, did he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Neither do I recall General Morillon or General Cordy-Simpson being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I may, to what you've referred to as the commanders' meeting of February 1st, 1993. The purpose of this meeting was what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, this is the meeting that you say an invitation was issued to Dario Kordic in both the capacity as a colonel, right, and as deputy president of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes. I can't recall the meeting, because I honestly don't recall at this stage whether it took place or not. I recall the invitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't attend the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I can't even remember if it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't even know whether Mr. Kordic participated in that meeting, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think he would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't recollect whether there was a meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was a -- well, by this time, the ceasefire agreement had actually already been signed, hadn't it? You had seen the order?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It didn't mean people weren't still shooting at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just show you an entry, if I may, from Lieutenant Colonel Robert A. Stewart's diary for that day and see if that jogs your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D56/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to turn your attention, sir, to the entry for Monday, the 1st of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second paragraph deals with this meeting which had apparently been called, supposedly, by Lieutenant General Morillon. Do you know whether it had been called by Lieutenant General Morillon or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I think it did, or was, rather, called by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is reference in here to the fact that it was clearly obvious that Lieutenant General Morillon had nothing further to add to what had already been agreed, that the conference was held for selfish reasons, and he wanted to associate himself with the ceasefire. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I know, but would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I wouldn't be in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who actually initiated this commanders' meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't remember at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, after February the 1st of 1993, could you just tell us where you were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I wouldn't know. Sometimes I was moving around, sometimes I was in the headquarters. I wouldn't have kept, I'm afraid, a daily record of where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the military situation just a few kilometres north of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would have been at the time, as far as we were informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You knew that the main road, the main arterial road, between Kiseljak and Busovaca and through Busovaca up to Zenica or to Vitez, off to the left, was actually cut off by a large Muslim checkpoint between the village of Kacuni and the village of Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I met them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That prevented communications between Busovaca and Kiseljak; didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: It certainly prevented road communications, yes. There were many occasions when, in all fairness, Dario Kordic would not have been able to get safely out of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also referred in your testimony to what you termed as reports, reports of some sort of a power struggle between Colonel Blaskic and Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't really have any personal knowledge of any such phenomenon, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not at all. I merely passed on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are not in a position to assess the credibility of those reports --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- or who actually made them, even?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't remember at this stage. I would have passed the reports back to our military information section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, who was the head of the civil government in the town that you spent five months in, Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I don't recall at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever met a gentleman by the name of Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I did once meet that gentleman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was in charge of Kiseljak, the civil government?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm not being evasive, but I genuinely do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the name of the HVO brigade that was stationed in Kiseljak was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not at this stage. I was just glad to get out of the whole situation. I didn't exactly wipe my mind blank, but I wouldn't have kept those small details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would be convenient, this might be a convenient time to break, and I'm delighted to report that I believe I only have about 15 minutes more of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Pinder, we're going to adjourn now. Could you be back at half past 2.00 for the rest of your examination. Would you remember, please, during this adjournment, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that includes, of course, the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pinder.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I know Mario Cerkez. I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pinder, when Dario Kordic arrived at the Mixed Military Working Group meeting on the 12th of December, 1992, and was introduced as "Colonel Dario Kordic," did he correct anyone and say, "Well, in fact you're wrong, I'm not a colonel"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When Mr. Kordic came -- Colonel Kordic came to the meeting between the 12th and 17th of December, 1992, on behalf of the HVO, did he correct anyone during that meeting and say, "I'm really not 'Colonel'"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm certain I would have recorded that had it been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he make any such correction at the meeting on the 17th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he never corrected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When he met with senior UNPROFOR officials and senior representatives of the Serbs and senior representatives of the Muslim BiH presidency, did he ever correct them and say, "I'm really not a colonel"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I would have to say that from the translations, I never heard him say that. But of course there were conversations that were not translated between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in the meetings themselves, when the minutes would be taken and the type of record that would be kept that we have seen at least one example of, as an official part of the meeting, did he ever go on record and say, "Really, for future reference, you should not address me as a colonel"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Exhibit 422.1, which is -- if the usher could ... The invitation, the fax to invite Colonel Kordic, also Vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, to this meeting on the 1st of February, 1993, and the attached letter, if I can direct your attention to the third page of Exhibit 422.1. Directing your attention to the address information in the upper left side, do I understand correctly it's your understanding that the Serbo-Croatian word "Pukovnik" is "Colonel"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the invitation to Colonel Kordic from UNPROFOR headquarters is to Pukovnik Dario Kordic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As part of, as you testified this morning, the inner command group of Brigadier Cordy-Simpson, to your knowledge, did Colonel Kordic ever contact anyone at UNPROFOR headquarters and say, "You probably should not send invitations to me addressed as 'Colonel Kordic'?"

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it ever come to your attention that Mr. Kordic was subsequently promoted to the rank of brigadier?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers asked you several questions about Colonel Bob Stewart's book. Referring to, for counsel, in the book, to page 77 of the book, would you agree with Colonel Stewart's position that Dario Kordic was an HVO military commander? Is that --

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: I think that's more or less what my opinion would be, from the time I was there. I have read Colonel Stewart's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you agree with Colonel Stewart's assessment on page 249 that Dario Kordic, the deputy president of the Croats, was also the commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you agree with Colonel Stewart's assessment at page 311 of his book that Dario Kordic was, quote, "a fanatic"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID NIGEL PINDER-KOEHNK
utterances.text: That was my initial assessment, yes. I didn't change that during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pinder, that concludes your evidence, and you are now released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Your Honour. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal first of all with the translation matter, because I have made inquiries of the registry and am informed that the procedure which we should follow is that the Defence should submit the areas which are in dispute, a document containing what is in dispute, and then the original or the current translation, plus the proposals, plus the tape, can go to the translators for review, and we'll get an answer back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Judge May, the Croatian version has already been identified to the Registrar, and it's page 5504 of the Prosecution's core documents, and the translation, which we believe to be an accurate translation, is page 5491 of the Prosecution's core documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be easier if you submit that formally with a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we'll ensure that the tape is submitted as well so that that can be listened to. The forecast of cross-examination taking three hours, plus the fact that the cross-examination of an earlier witness was postponed, means that I don't have another witness immediately available for you this afternoon. I can qualify that in a minute. The next witness, Colonel Watters, who is due to start tomorrow morning at half past 9.00, doesn't get in until later this afternoon, and obviously I can't take him. I've had, as a form of reserve, a witness who works in the institution called Payam Akhavan. I've told my learned friends about him, and he's very substantially prepared for the giving of evidence but he's not immediately available, and if it's possible to call him, say, in chief this afternoon, I might be able to do that starting at about a quarter past 3.00 and thus perhaps use an hour of time. But I have, first of all, finally to track him down and also to check that the summary that has been prepared in draft is one with which he agrees. It may need a few minor alterations. I think all that's probably being worked on at the moment, but until I leave the room, I can't know whether it would be possible to take him, as I suggest, in chief this afternoon, with the balance of his evidence and cross-examination perhaps deferred to a later date. It might be Friday morning, if Colonel Watters finishes in a day, or it might be one day next week when there will be some difficulties about filling the two and a half days with evidence. When I say "difficulties", difficulties more in the timetabling than in the quantity of evidence, I think. So I'm in the Chamber's hands as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Three days next week, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've only got a half day on Tuesday, we were informed. Monday, half day Tuesday, Wednesday, and then a status conference all day Thursday. That's what we were told at one stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can seek the Chamber's views on calling evidence, if it's available this afternoon for an hour, to use the time most efficiently. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear the witness, if available, at 3.15. We would normally prefer to get the cross-examination in as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason I make the different proposal, namely, that his cross-examination might be deferred, is that Colonel Watters is a witness whose testimony is likely to be a little longer than the witness yesterday or today and therefore could extend beyond one day. He has to go back to England on Friday, and, in any event, we would finish evidence on Friday at lunchtime. He's not resident in the institution. It seemed to me perhaps preferable that we should give priority to concluding Colonel Watters' evidence by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we'll follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I, before the Chamber adjourns, mention two things? First, just generally, the status conference that the Chamber has said is for next Thursday and all day, might we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case again we misunderstood you, because we thought if it was going to be all day, we couldn't immediately forecast why it was going to take all day, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The proposal is that at the end, possibly, of that day, provided there's time, we might review things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case that's very helpful. We'll work on the basis which we provisionally allowed for, that some or the majority of Thursday is available for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Two matters to correct, if I may. They both arise from questions asked by the Defence on the basis of documents that were referred to but which were not produced. It's unfortunate when errors creep in, for although, of course, it's the answers that count, the words of the question sometimes linger in the mind. On the 22nd of September [sic], as the final question of Mr. Donia, I think, Mr. Stein said: "Were you aware that Colonel Stewart also told us that the HVO was totally unprepared for the events in the Lasva Valley on April the 15th?" What Colonel Stewart actually said was restricted to Zenica, because he was asked a question about Zenica: "Were they prepared for conflict with the BH army to begin on the morning of the 16th of April or were they not prepared?" His answer was, "I don't know the answer, but I can give an opinion. My opinion was that the kidnapping of the man called Totic came as a severe shock to the HVO, and the HVO brigade commander, the second one, was extremely concerned, so I suspect that my opinion was the answer is 'No'." Question: "But they were not prepared; is that correct?" Answer: "That is correct. It's an opinion, it's not my fact." So that related specifically to Zenica. The second correction relates to a document referred to initially as an ECMM document by Mr. Sayers a couple of days ago in which it was suggested that by 1993, there were 2,1 million refugees in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document was in fact a document of the Commission of Human Rights and neither the ECMM document initially referred to or a different version of the document subsequently identified, and it was not a question of there being 2,1 million refugees in Bosnia-Herzegovina by 1993, for what the report said at paragraph 13 of introductory remarks was that: "Over 2,1 million people have been displaced from their homes since the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina began, nearly 50 per cent of the population recorded in the census of 1991. Some 800.000 of them are estimated to have sought refuge outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. The rest are seeking refuge inside the country. Tens of thousands have gone to save areas such as Gorazde, Zepce, Srebrenica, Tuzla, Bihac and Sarajevo," and that is the way the document actually recorded matters. Your Honour, if I find that I am incapable of locating or dealing with the witness by 3.15, would you prefer that I deal with it formally or informally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Send word through. Otherwise, we'll sit again at 3.15. But before we do and while it's in my mind, let me mention some revisions for the calendar in the autumn brought about by my having to sit on another case. I shall not be available to sit on this case in the mornings of the 8th to the 10th of November. We shall sit the afternoons of those days only, and of course we will sit as normal on the 11th and 12th. That's November. In October, I shall now be available in the mornings of the weeks beginning the 11th of October and the 18th of October, so we will be sitting the mornings of those two weeks as well as the afternoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've been told that Payam Akhavan is available. There are summaries for the Court, copies for the Defence. May I, nevertheless, have until 3.15 just to check a couple of exhibits with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry we've kept you. We were engaged in another matter. Yes, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, relevant recent education, and employment, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, relevant recent education, and relevant recent employment, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: My full name is Payam Akhavan. I'm presently legal advisor with the Office of the Prosecutor. I have law degrees from Osgoode Hall Law School in Toronto, Canada, and from Harvard Law School in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before working, as we know you did, as a United Nations human rights officer, what had been your then most recent employment?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Prior to joining the United Nations Centre for Human Rights, I was working at the Danish Centre for Human Rights in Copenhagen; and in my capacity as expert, I was appointed to two missions of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, both dealing with investigations of humanitarian law violations in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What period of time did those missions occupy?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: They occupied a period roughly from September of 1992 to April of 1993, when I joined the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For that work, did you have any training? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, well, these were both high-level missions, and I was appointed to these missions by the European Community presidency. The preparation for these missions involved extensive debriefing sessions with Foreign Ministry officials, various officials who were situated on the ground in the former Yugoslavia, and of course the experience gained through the mission itself, which involved meeting various officials, investigating various sites where alleged atrocities had taken place, and the preparation of analytical reports for submission to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So with that education and background, on the 30th of April of 1993, you were working for the United Nations as a human rights officer in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you tasked with on-site investigations of human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was hired specifically in order to open a field operation in the former Yugoslavia for the then-U.N. Human Rights Commission Special Rapporteur for the former Yugoslavia, Prime Minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki of Poland. My colleague and I at that time were responsible for monitoring human rights violations in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and to send reports back to Geneva for incorporation in reports which were submitted to the Commission on Human Rights periodically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your colleague at the time being ... ?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas Osorio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1993, where were you precisely, and initially what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe that we arrived in Sarajevo on the 30th of April, in the evening -- I'm sorry; we arrived in Sarajevo and were taken to Vitez that same evening. And on May the 1st, the members of the British Battalion who were responsible for our presence in the region took us on a tour of Vitez, Ahmici, to give us an overview of the destruction which had taken place. We also were debriefed by members of the British Battalion about their general impressions of the situation in the Vitez region. What we observed during the first day was extensive destruction of property --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pause for a minute. Before we come to what you observed, was it a question of your being debriefed or briefed by the British Battalion? And which officers by name, or other ranks by name, spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we were at that point trying to develop general familiarity with the situation in the region, so we asked pertinent questions, largely from Bryan Watters, who was, I believe, a sergeant within the ranks of the British Battalion; to a certain extent, Colonel Stewart, Bob Stewart; as well as other members, including the padre of the British Battalion, and other soldiers whose names I can't recall. And our purpose for that particular day was to get, as I said, a general impression of what the situation was in the Vitez region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter of detail before we turn to paragraph 3 of the summary: What was Watters' rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe it was major, or sergeant; I don't recall. I recall the name but not the rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry if they didn't reach the Court; I distributed them before the short break, but it may be that if the Court was occupied on other business, it couldn't have read them in advance in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I am down to paragraph 3, but I'm correcting the rank attributed to Watters in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I recall that he was the second in command --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: -- from Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You saw damaged property; tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, on the 1st of May, we visited Vitez, and we drove around Ahmici but did not actually enter the village. We saw extensive damage to homes. The evening before, when we had arrived in Vitez in the evening, we had also seen, driving into the city, a number of homes being put on fire. In Ahmici, we also noticed that there were several soldiers we saw from a distance who were apparently looting property from homes which had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you given an account of casualties in Vitez during the attack?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We were told by the padre, who had been involved in facilitating the burial of several casualties, that there had been in the Vitez municipality, as opposed to outlying areas, approximately 5 Croatian dead and 96 Muslim dead. And he knew that based on his involvement in facilitating the return of the bodies and their burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From Vitez to Ahmici itself, you've spoken of the looters; did anybody suggest who the looters were?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The members of the British Battalion seemed to think that they were the local HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you see from your position whether the looters were in civilian clothes or uniform?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: They appeared to be wearing military fatigue, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the level of damage or destruction to properties and other -- domestic properties and other buildings in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The level of damage was extensive. This is something which we appreciated more fully after May the 1st, when on subsequent occasions we visited the village of Ahmici and were engaged in a much more thorough investigation. It appeared that the overwhelming majority of homes and property in the village had been destroyed; almost all had been burnt. In certain cases it appeared as if they had been burnt using some sort of flammable liquid, perhaps petrol, and that was apparent by the dark charcoal colour left behind in various buildings. All animals --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to just interrupt you for this purpose: On the 1st of May, then, a somewhat distant view of the village; your next return on what day?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe that the return was on the 2nd or 3rd of May, and there was a return about two days after that together with the European Community ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can partition your memory up into what you saw on that first return the 2nd or 3rd of May and tell us what you saw there, so much the better. In addition to seeing damage to property, and you've described by what method the property appeared to have been damaged, did you see any evidence of the nature of the attack in the forms of shells, bullets, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: You refer here to May the 1st?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the 2nd or 3rd.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I see. Our impression was, based on explanations given to us by members of the British Battalion and based on the physical evidence that was available and based on subsequent interviews with victims, that the attack on the village had commenced early in the morning on April the 16th, possibly at 5.30 or 6.00 in the morning, and that the attack had commenced from the main road, the Vitez-to-Busovaca road, which crosses Ahmici. There was evidence that artillery fire had been used in order to scare many of the inhabitants from leaving their homes into the open, where they were shot. There was evidence that mortar shells had been used, that rocket-propelled grenades had been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What evidence was there that you yourself saw, as opposed to evidence related to you by others?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, the evidence were the spent casings, shell casings of mortar rounds and rocket-propelled grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one objection, Your Honour, if I may to this line of questioning. I think what the Prosecution is trying to do is to elicit from one of their employees military opinions, and I don't believe that they have adequately laid a foundation for this gentleman's possession of any military expertise whatsoever. In fact, his testimony is to the reverse, and therefore I think that he's just expressing opinions without any foundation or competence to be able to do that, rather than telling the Court about facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The characterisation of this witness as an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor is unworthy, irrelevant, and inappropriate. The witness will deal with his expertise later. At the moment, he's dealing with evidence of fact, what he found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the Tribunal find -- I'm sorry not to have given advance notice -- the map of Ahmici, which is Z1585,1. It's not a map, it's an aerial view. If the witness is allowed to mark the copy on the ELMO at present, then that will, of course, become a different exhibit number, but we can replace the original exhibit with another one in unmarked form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the things that you found was in the area, I think, of a cemetery. Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. First of all, with a marker, if you would be so good, and I'm not sure which one shows up better -- it may be the bright orange one is better than the purple one. Try the purple one. You may be right. Can you just put a mark for where the cemetery is?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Is that sufficiently clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. What was it that you found there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, across the road from the cemetery in this location approximately where you, I think, can see a sort of depression (indicating), we found a large number of spent shell casings apparently from a gun, a machine gun, whatever the case may be. And in the proximity of this area, somewhere in this field where I've marked an "X" (indicating), the members of the British Battalion had found, I believe, 20 or so bodies, and their impression was that many of these people who were fleeing their homes after the artillery fire began had been ambushed in this area and had been shot by snipers. So the spent casings which we found in this depression or hollow, which would appear to be an ideal place for them to hide, gave us an indication that that may have been where they had shot the 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What approximate number of shell cases did you find?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I would say anywhere from 150 to 200, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The size of the spent shell cases? If you're able, from expertise or experience, to give a technical definition, do so. If you're not, use your fingers and show us how big.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it would take too much expertise to figure out the difference between the spent casing from a rifle or machine gun and that from a rocket-propelled grenade. On average, the spent shell casings coming from ordinary weapons would be to the tune of, I would say, four, five centimetres, something to that effect (indicating). There were also much larger casings which we were told belonged to anti-aircraft machine guns which for some reason were often used, and they tended to be somewhat larger. But I think in terms of the cases from rocket-propelled grenades or from mortars, they were considerably bigger, and it was very clear that they could be distinguished from ordinary weapons such as machine guns or rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see, yourself, or handle any of the casings apparently associated with anti-aircraft machine guns?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, approximately, with your fingers or by size, what size were they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I would say they were anything from one and a half to two times the size of an ordinary bullet coming from a rifle. I would say their casings were roughly this big (indicating). I'm not sure if that is ten centimetres or thereabouts. And they were, of course, also much wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then finally, did you see, yourself, cases from any rocket-propelled grenades or mortars at any time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case the Tribunal needs assistance, approximately what size are the casings of those shells?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The rocket-propelled grenades, to the best of my recollection, were probably so big (indicating), the spent shell casings. I don't know, 15, 20 centimetres. Mortar shells tended to be more or less the same size, sometimes bigger, but I think often it was also a question of their width. I, of course, was instructed by the soldiers who accompanied us, and they would very often explain to us what the difference is between the various casings. Our main concern was to try and understand how the attack had taken place, what was the pattern of victimisation, and who was responsible. In the nature of a human rights investigation, one is not dealing with individual criminal accountability. One does not pay heed perhaps to the same details as one would in a criminal context. But what we had to prove to our satisfaction was that people were killed not in combat but as a result of the deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects, and then to determine which party to the conflict was responsible for those atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn back to your account of events that day and in order not to overlook it, can you just mark a "C" beside the outline that you've given for the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then indicate the small circle beneath the cemetery -- between the cemetery and the mark "X" is the small hollow you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You needn't mark that further. Was there a smell?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was apparent that there were still bodies under the rubble. There was a stench of rotting flesh which I think came both from the livestock and other animals, dogs and cats, all of the animals which had been killed, some of which somehow were still alive several days after the event. But as we found out subsequently, there were also still human bodies in the remains of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you and Thomas Osorio approach three apparent local residents at one stage?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. As we were going from house to house, trying to assess the damage, we noticed that there was an old lady with two young boys walking through the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able, from the plan or on the plan, to tell us with any precision where this was?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was somewhere in this general area (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would mark that with a circle, if you're no more precise about it than that.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case we're going to have further markings on this plan, can you just put a "1" beside that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you approached this woman and the two young boys, were you alone or in company with any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We were alone. The soldiers remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How far behind?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I would say between 150 to 200 metres. We had been wandering through the village for some time, and the soldiers were, I think, on the road around their APCs somewhere in this area which I've marked "X".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We were wearing civilian clothes, but in particular we had a blue -- light blue flak jackets, which was, of course, the U.N. colour, if you like, together with U.N. arm bands and a blue U.N. helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were the soldiers from the U.N. dressed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The soldiers from the U.N. were in their military fatigues but also wearing -- I don't recall if they were wearing U.N. helmets or not, but they were in their military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you and Thomas Osorio dressed effectively identically? If not identically, were you similarly dressed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would put Thomas Osorio beside one of the United Nations uniformed soldiers, would you have been able to tell the difference between one and the other, in terms of uniform and clothing?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The woman and the two boys, when you approached them, was there any other person, and in particular was there any other soldier or any soldier anywhere near them?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No. We virtually saw no one in the village because most of the homes had been destroyed, and one of the reasons why our curiosity was aroused is exactly because there were so few people that we could speak with in order to get some sort of possible explanation as to what had transpired on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you spoke to them, or perhaps earlier, -- I'm not sure, you must tell us -- when you approached them, did something happen?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: My colleague, Thomas Osorio, approached them, since he was a translator and could speak the local language, and I stayed a few metres behind, also in part because there was a television crew which was trying to follow us, and I was trying to discourage them from following us. At that point, we heard some sort of gunfire, and we realised that we were being targeted by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able then to locate where the snipers may have been?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It was very difficult to determine specifically where they were firing from, but based on the direction of the bullets, it was possible to get a general idea where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you now translate that general idea on to this map, or not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the bullets were coming -- I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think -- we've used one; you put a little cross above one, but we'll leave that. If you now go to the next area and use a figure "2" to mark it.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The area where the bullets were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The snipers were, apparently.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is roughly the direction (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've drawn two arrows some 30 or more degrees apart?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, because it was difficult to tell specifically where they were coming from, and based on the direction of the bullets, they could have come from anywhere within those two arrows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would put a "2" beside each of those arrows. You have put it beside one at the moment, I think and on the other arrow as well, the one to the right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is a "2" there. It's probably not visible, but there is a "2" there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How near did these bullets get to you, as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, there were several bullets fired, and since we had to run some way in an open field to get to the APC, I think the snipers had an opportunity to fire several times. Some of them came to us as close as maybe half a metre, or possibly closer. It was difficult to tell under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as you were running to the APC, did you come to be closer to any soldiers, or were there no soldiers until you got to the APC?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: There were no soldiers until we got very close to the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And apart from you in blue helmets and other U.N.-attired soldiers, were there any other soldiers around, or any other people in military or apparent military uniform?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: None that we could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your sources of information for what had happened at Ahmici were what?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The sources of information included international peacekeeping forces, such as the British Battalion, as well as members of the U.N. High Commission for Refugees, on some occasions nongovernmental organisations, media people, others who had been in the area and had some familiarity; but of course, first and foremost, in the case of Ahmici, they included the survivors who we managed to interview in Zenica at a refugee camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to the product of your inquiry in due course. Did you visit the survivors in Zenica before your third visit, which you think was, I think, on the 4th of May or thereabouts, or was it only after that that you visited and spoke to the survivors?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We visited the survivors in between our second and third visits. The first visit allowed us to familiarise ourselves with the physical context and evidence of the humanitarian law violations, following which we interviewed a number of survivors, which allowed us to go back to the village on a third occasion, together with three European Community ambassadors who happened to be on mission at that time. And based on -- based on instructions which we were given by one of the survivors, we were actually able to locate a home in which we found the remains of four individuals who apparently had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to put everything in its sequence, if I can, and we'll come to that in its proper place. On, then, the second visit -- that's on the 2nd or 3rd of May -- you approached the old lady or the lady and the two boys. Just "Yes" or "No": Was she able to give you any information at any stage?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, she was reluctant to speak with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you speak on that occasion to any other villagers, or not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: No, there were no other villagers that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Zenica, approximately what number of survivors did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I, of course, spoke to fewer survivors than my colleague, Thomas Osorio, who spent more time there and who returned, actually, on one occasion. I would say I had spoken to anywhere from 10 to 20 survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did Thomas Osorio's information, or did the information he gathered from the people to whom he spoke, did that come to you? Did the two of you share information you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we were part of a team, so we readily shared all the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to the product of your inquiries and your visit to the village, on the 4th of May, did you also visit another village, Miletici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court finds this exhibit, which is 2612,2, helpful, we may be marking it. If I can just lay mine on the ELMO, we'll get the usher to help me, for a reason that will become obvious. Rather than to corrupt -- just leave it there; that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the map with the yellow sticker and the red arrow on it, serving the purpose simply of identifying a village, is that Miletici, the village, or indeed hamlet, to which you went?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct. That is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the camera could now be -- or if a wider view of the map could now be shown, then we'll see the relationship of Miletici to, first, Zenica, and can you point out on this map Ahmici for us, please, Mr. Akhavan? It may be a bit further down, even, sir. You may have to open it up.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, here is Busovaca, so I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you move it up a bit more and just point to Busovaca, that will do, I think, for the purposes of reminding the Tribunal of the relevant geography. There is Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Here -- here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then going back up, we see that Miletici is to the northwest of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, at Miletici, conduct an inquiry to discover what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we visited Miletici, which was a hamlet in which a number of Croatian inhabitants were living. And apparently there had been an attack on that hamlet, not in the form of an assault, but in the form of three or so young Croatian men being taken out of their homes, tortured, and beheaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the perpetrators of this atrocity being, apparently, who?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: According to the local inhabitants, they were the so-called Mujahedins, which, according to what we gathered, were a combination of foreign mercenaries and local extremists who engaged in these sort of atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing now with the accounts you received from survivors in Ahmici, did you and Mr. Osorio look for points of similarity, and indeed for points of inconsistency and dissimilarity in the accounts given?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that was a standard method by which we established the veracity of testimony. We generally would ask a number of people apart from each other, so they could not necessarily share the same story, their version of the events, often focusing on specific details such as when, for example, the firing began in that morning; in which location certain people were killed; so on and so forth. And we were satisfied that the stories were, for the most part, quite consistent and credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us part of that account at an earlier stage. What was the account of who mounted the attack?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: According to basically all the witnesses that we spoke with, those who mounted the attack were members of the HVO. And many of them were able to identify particular individuals by name who were either from their own village, in Ahmici, or from neighbouring villages. So in addition to being able to identify the HVO insignia on the uniforms of those who were performing the attacks, I believe we collected about 18 or 20 specific names. Of course it was not our task to gather individual names; we were not involved in a criminal investigation. But we gathered those names in any event, in order to establish in our subsequent meetings with HVO leaders that indeed, the victims could identify particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any of the accounts point to any other grouping apart from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We did not receive any information to that effect from the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit Blaskic in Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe it was the 4th or 5th of May, to the best of my recollection. It was towards the end of our stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got there, what, if any, military presence was there at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: There were quite a few soldiers in front and inside the building. Some of them were wearing ordinary military uniforms; others were wearing a distinctive black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How easy or difficult was it to have a meeting with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: It was not terribly difficult. I think that the British Battalion had arranged a meeting, and we didn't really encounter any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you summarise, please, what was said by him, giving questions asked by you, if appropriate, about the Ahmici attack?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll object to that, Your Honour, on the grounds of hearsay. We have no access to Colonel Blaskic, for the same reasons that we had no access to Zlatko Aleksovski. So I object to trying to get in through the back door what they should not be able to get in through the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What difference does that make in terms of hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, it's hearsay because we have no opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's hearsay, and it's admitted in the Tribunal, as you know. Now, what is the particular point of the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have no means of being able to test whether or not this gentleman actually said what this witness is going to say that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can go and ask Colonel Blaskic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, can you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Colonel -- then-Colonel Blaskic firstly about the structure of the military in that region, what was the zone of his control, and what were the armed forces which were under his command. He explained to me, in general terms, that he was responsible for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and that he was in clear control of that area, despite the existence of certain irregular elements, such as the HOS, and other paramilitary formations. I then discussed with him what we had seen at Ahmici, explaining to him that apparently a large number of civilians had been killed and that virtually all Muslim homes and property had been destroyed, and asked him for an explanation. The reason for my meeting with Colonel Blaskic and other Bosnian Croat leaders in the region was to afford them an opportunity to provide their version of events, so that the eventual report which we submitted to the U.N. Human Rights Commission would have heard both sides and would have been in a position to be balanced, fair, and impartial. Colonel Blaskic at no time admitted that his soldiers were in any way involved in the attack, but at the same time was not willing to offer any explanations as to who was responsible. He simply denied that he or his soldiers had anything to do with it but did not respond in any credible fashion to the fact that, according to all the available testimony, members of the HVO had been responsible for the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the question of investigating the attack raised?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Meaning to say ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Investigating locally.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I had informed Colonel Blaskic, as I did on all occasions when I met commanders, that it was his responsibility to investigate the matter and to ensure that those who were responsible are brought to justice, and that his failure to do so would result in his criminal liability. Of course, this was not, strictly speaking, part of our mandate, as I've explained on several occasions. We were not engaged in a criminal investigation. The mandate of a human rights Special Rapporteur is to look, in general, at state responsibility; and where state responsibility cannot be established in the context of armed conflict, where there are several para-state entities who have perhaps de facto control of an area but which are not legitimate states or governments, one has to look at which party to the conflict controlled a particular area and which party to the conflict may have been responsible. So the emphasis of my questions was to try and determine whether there was any other plausible explanation other than the one offered by all witnesses, that the HVO had been responsible. But part of the mandate of the human rights Special Rapporteur also was to engage in preventive action which, in many respects, involved persuading local villagers to enforce humanitarian law principles, if necessary through conducting investigations and prosecuting those responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some time later, did you see a man called Ante Valenta?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that during the meeting with Colonel Blaskic, somewhere in the middle, Mr. Valenta joined us, and he briefly interjected --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His contribution being to what effect?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: His contribution largely being a dose of apparently what happened to be the official ideology of the HDZ or HVO regarding the -- the presence of the Muslims in the area, and how the Muslims had different values from the Christian Croats, and how they were a menace and somehow uncivilised peoples who had to be gotten rid of, in general terms, and at one point, Mr. Valenta suggested that although the International Community was often condemning acts of brutality against Muslims, that in reality there was sympathy throughout Europe for getting rid of Turks and Muslims and others who really did not belong in the European civilisation. That was, in essence, what I got from his intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How, if at all, was his intervention linked to the attack you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it gave us a sense of the general policy or attitude prevailing at the time, and of course others were not as outspoken as Mr. Valenta. Others would be much more subtle or apologetic. But the clear sense was that there was considerable animosity against the Muslims in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this witness's evidence is to be -- I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was going to raise the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness's evidence is to be broken in any event, and in light of the content of paragraph 15, this might be a sensible moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me to discuss with my learned friends opposite their probable time for cross-examination of the witness Watters who comes next, and assuming that both Mr. Watters and Mr. Akhavan are fully available tomorrow morning, it may be that it would be preferable to continue with this evidence in chief if there's a realistic prospect of what is being concluded in the balance of the time to the end of the week. Alternatively, I would seek your leave tomorrow morning to interject Watters in order to complete him in a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, the next witness has to be considered in terms of his availability. But, on the other hand, if we can finish this witness in chief, so much the better, I should have thought. There is one other matter, that the air-conditioning seems totally to have failed. I will ask the registrar to take the matter up on our behalf again, please. Mr. Akhavan, you are giving evidence. Would you please remember, in this adjournment and any others there may be, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that, of course, includes the members of the Prosecution here, apart from matters concerning your own availability and the arrangements. Thank you. If you would be back otherwise when you're asked. We'll adjourn now until half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
